'''Anquan Kenmile Boldin''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|æ|n|k|w|ɑː|n}}; born October 3, 1980) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for 14 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State Seminoles]] and was selected by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] in the second round of the [[2003 NFL draft]]. He also played for the [[Baltimore Ravens]], [[San Francisco 49ers]] and [[Detroit Lions]].

Boldin was the 2003 [[NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year]], was selected to three [[Pro Bowls]] and won [[Super Bowl XLVII]] with the Ravens. In 2015, he was named the [[Walter Payton Man of the Year]] for his community service.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gutierrez |first=Paul |date=February 7, 2016 |title=Anquan Boldin named Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year |url=https://www.espn.co.uk/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/197879/anquan-boldin-named-walter-payton-nfl-man-of-the-year |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230422170544/https://tags.bluekai.com/site/24765?ret=html&phint=pageName%3Despnuk%3Anfl%3Ablog&phint=channel%3Despnuk%3Anfl&phint=eVar34%3D&phint=events%3Devent3&phint=prop1%3Despnuk&phint=swid%3D63A8E90C-9219-4BA8-CB7F-B00E388990CB&phint=unid&phint=prop4%3Dblog&phint=prop9%3Dstory%3Ascroll%2Bnext_story&phint=prop23%3Dlouis-jacques_marcel&phint=prop25%3Dfootball&phint=prop26%3Dnfl&phint=prop30%3Dpremium-no&phint=prop32%3D&phint=prop45%3D&phint=__bk_t%3DDolphins%27%20Jaelan%20Phillips%2C%20teammates%20inspired%20by%20mentoring%20incarcerated%20teens%20-%20NFL%20Nation-%20ESPN&phint=__bk_k%3D&phint=__bk_l%3Dhttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.espn.co.uk%2Fblog%2Fnflnation%2Fpost%2F_%2Fid%2F320436%2Fdolphins-jaelan-phillips-teammates-inspired-by-mentoring-incarcerated-teens&phint=__bk_v%3D3.1.10&limit=10&r=15147166 |archive-date=April 22, 2023 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref> Despite not being named to the [[National Football League 2000s All-Decade Team|NFL 2000s All-Decade Team]], Boldin is widely considered as one of the greatest wide receivers of his era.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 23, 2016 |title=#9 Anquan Boldin {{!}} Top 10 Wide Receivers of the 2000s {{!}} NFL Films |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=StCx1XKMptk |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220816065437/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=StCx1XKMptk |archive-date=August 16, 2022 |access-date=August 16, 2022 |website=YouTube.com |publisher=NFL Films |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life==
Boldin played football, [[basketball]], and ran track at [[Pahokee High School]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Evenson |first=John |date=November 25, 2019 |title=Retired NFL star Anquan Boldin shares his many passions at alma mater Pahokee H.S. |url=https://cbs12.com/sports/content/retired-nfl-star-anquan-boldin-shares-his-many-passions-at-alma-mater-pahokee-hs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191222110218/https://cbs12.com/sports/content/retired-nfl-star-anquan-boldin-shares-his-many-passions-at-alma-mater-pahokee-hs |archive-date=December 22, 2019 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=CBS12.com |language=en}}</ref> His ability playing as a [[quarterback]] led him to be named [[Florida]]'s [[Mr. Football Award (Florida)|Mr. Football]] in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anquan Boldin |url=http://www.seminoles.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/boldin_anquan00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120503132627/http://www.seminoles.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/boldin_anquan00.html |archive-date=May 3, 2012 |access-date=January 16, 2013 |website=Florida State University Official Athletic Site}}. Seminoles.com. Retrieved on February 4, 2013.</ref> During his senior season, Pahokee held a 10–0 regular season record including a 34–14 win over [[Glades Central High School|Glades Central]] in the annual Muck Bowl.<ref>{{Cite web |last=George |first=Dave |date=November 13, 1998 |title=Pahokee takes turn in muck; after a few tense moments, Boldin has the needed pluck |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/sports/high-school/1998/11/14/pahokee-takes-turn-in-muck/7153162007/ |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=The Palm Beach Post |language=en-US}}</ref>  After the season, he was a [[USA Today]] first-team selection and named ''Florida Player of the Year''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roberts |first=Mike |date=September 8, 2022 |title=Anquan Boldin: One of NFL's greats on and off football field |url=https://bvmsports.com/2022/09/08/anquan-boldin-one-of-nfls-greats-on-and-off-football-field/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220910160109/https://bvmsports.com/2022/09/08/anquan-boldin-one-of-nfls-greats-on-and-off-football-field/ |archive-date=September 10, 2022 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=BVM Sports |language=en-US}}</ref>

Also a standout [[track and field|track]] athlete, Boldin competed in sprinting, jumping and throwing events at Pahokee High. He was timed at 52.34 seconds over [[400 meters]]. In jumps, he recorded a personal-best leap of 6.13 meters in the [[long jump]]. As a thrower, he got a top-throw of 13.53 meters in the [[shot put]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anquan Boldin – Florida State – Cardinals WR |url=https://www.trackingfootball.com/players/anquan-boldin-11407/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304023905/https://www.trackingfootball.com/players/anquan-boldin-11407/ |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |website=Tracking Football}}</ref>

In 2007, he was named to the [[FHSAA's All-Century Team|Florida High School Association All-Century Team]], a team compiled of the top 33 players in the 100-year history of high school football in the state of Florida.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 13, 2007 |title=FHSAA's All-Century Team |url=https://www.theledger.com/story/news/2007/12/13/fhsaas-all-century-team/25867144007/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230422170620/https://www.theledger.com/story/news/2007/12/13/fhsaas-all-century-team/25867144007/ |archive-date=April 22, 2023 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=The Ledger |language=en-US}}</ref>

==College career==
Boldin attended [[Florida State University]] from 1999 to 2002. In the 2002 season, he had nine receptions for 175 receiving yards against [[2002 Notre Dame Fighting Irish football team|Notre Dame]], a three-touchdown game against [[2002 North Carolina Tar Heels football team|North Carolina]], and a two-touchdown game against [[Florida–Florida State football rivalry|rival]] [[2002 Florida Gators football team|Florida]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Notre Dame at Florida State Box Score, October 26, 2002 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-10-26-florida-state.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230407101541/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-10-26-florida-state.html |archive-date=April 7, 2023 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=North Carolina at Florida State Box Score, November 16, 2002 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-11-16-florida-state.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170723015837/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-11-16-florida-state.html |archive-date=July 23, 2017 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Florida at Florida State Box Score, November 30, 2002 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-11-30-florida-state.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170722090122/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/2002-11-30-florida-state.html |archive-date=July 22, 2017 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He was converted to [[wide receiver]] in order to get more playing time. In 23 games at wide receiver, he caught 118 passes for 1,790 yards (averaging 15.2 yards per reception) and 21 touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anquan Boldin College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/anquan-boldin-1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017103127/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/anquan-boldin-1.html |archive-date=October 17, 2022 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

==Professional career==

===Pre-draft===
Boldin created initial concerns of the NFL scouts after he registered a relatively slow 4.7 time in the [[40-yard dash]] at the [[NFL Scouting Combine|NFL Combine]].<ref name="SI.com - 2003 NFL - Draft Preview">{{Cite news |date=February 24, 2003 |title=SI.com – 2003 NFL – Draft Preview |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2003/draft/news/2003/02/23/combine_sunday/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090123073050/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2003/draft/news/2003/02/23/combine_sunday/ |archive-date=January 23, 2009 |access-date=August 21, 2008 |work=CNN}}</ref>

===Arizona Cardinals===

====2003 season====

[[File:Anquan Boldin 9-7-08.jpg|thumb|180px|Boldin spent seven seasons with the [[Arizona Cardinals]] from 2003 to 2009 and was voted to three [[Pro Bowl]]s during his tenure with the team. Here he is shown in September 2008.]]

====2004 season====
Boldin suffered a right knee injury in training camp.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 11, 2004 |title=Cards' Boldin injured |url=https://www.heraldtribune.com/story/news/2004/08/11/cards-boldin-injured/28820305007/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230422170604/https://www.heraldtribune.com/story/news/2004/08/11/cards-boldin-injured/28820305007/ |archive-date=April 22, 2023 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |website=Sarasota Herald-Tribune |language=en-US}}</ref> He was inactive for the first six regular season games. In the 2004 season, Boldin finished with 56 receptions for 623 receiving yards and one receiving touchdown in ten games. He had two games going over 100 receiving yards on the year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anquan Boldin 2004 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BoldAn00/gamelog/2004/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201002211127/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BoldAn00/gamelog/2004/ |archive-date=October 2, 2020 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

====2005 season====
In Week 2, against the [[2005 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams]], Boldin had eight receptions for 119 receiving yards in the 17–12 loss.<ref>{{Cite web |title=St. Louis Rams at Arizona Cardinals – September 18th, 2005 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200509180crd.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017020521/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200509180crd.htm |archive-date=October 17, 2022 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In Week 4, against [[2005 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco]], he had eight receptions for 116 receiving yards and a touchdown in the 31–14 victory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=San Francisco 49ers at Arizona Cardinals – October 2nd, 2005 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200510020crd.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221204210706/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200510020crd.htm |archive-date=December 4, 2022 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In the following game, against the [[2005 Carolina Panthers season|Carolina Panthers]], he had ten receptions for 162 receiving yards and a receiving touchdown in the 24–20 loss.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carolina Panthers at Arizona Cardinals – October 9th, 2005 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200510090crd.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018230520/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200510090crd.htm |archive-date=October 18, 2022 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In Week 11, Boldin started a streak of five consecutive games going over the 100-yard mark. Arguably his finest moment came against the [[2005 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]] on December 4 when he broke several tackles and scored the game-winning touchdown in a 17–10 win. He had 11 receptions for 156 receiving yards on the day.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arizona Cardinals at San Francisco 49ers – December 4th, 2005 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200512040sfo.htm |url-status=live Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=December 5, 2005 |title=Warner, Boldin power Cards past Smith, Niners |url=http://espn.go.com/nfl/recap?gameId=251204025 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303225830/http://espn.go.com/nfl/recap?gameId=251204025 |archive-date=March 3, 2016 |access-date=April 22, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> In Week 15 against the [[2005 Houston Texans season|Houston Texans]], he had eight receptions for 134 receiving yards and one receiving touchdown in the 30–19 loss.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arizona Cardinals at Houston Texans – December 18th, 2005 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200512180htx.htm |url-status=live ====2008 season====
On September 28, 2008, Boldin was carted off the field after a violent [[helmet-to-helmet]] collision in the end zone with 27 seconds remaining in the Cardinals' 56–35 loss to the [[2008 New York Jets|New York Jets]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 28, 2008 |title=Cardinals' Boldin carted off field after hit to head |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3614514 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220407001323/https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3614514 |archive-date=April 7, 2022 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |language=en |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> While attempting to catch a long pass from [[Kurt Warner]], Boldin was hit in the back by free safety [[Kerry Rhodes]] and then took an illegal helmet-to-face shot from strong safety [[Eric Smith (safety)|Eric Smith]], knocking them both unconscious. Smith was able to get up after a few moments. After several minutes, Boldin was placed on a stretcher and carted off the field. Smith was fined $50,000 and suspended one game. Boldin left the game having caught 10 passes for 119 yards and a touchdown.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arizona Cardinals at New York Jets – September 28th, 2008 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200809280nyj.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190226030256/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200809280nyj.htm |archive-date=February 26, 2019 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>  On October 4, 2008, coach Ken Whisenhunt announced that Boldin would be out for an indefinite time period with fractured [[paranasal sinuses]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 4, 2008 |title=Cardinals WR Boldin undergoes surgery to repair facial fracture |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3625384 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081005182805/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/news/story?id=3625384 |archive-date=October 5, 2008 |access-date=October 4, 2008 |website=ESPN.com |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> Boldin returned three weeks later. He had 13 receptions for 186 receiving yards in a 26–20 victory over the [[2008 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] in Week 11.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arizona Cardinals at Seattle Seahawks – November 16th, 2008 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200811160sea.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221013225127/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200811160sea.htm |archive-date=October 13, 2022 |access-date=April 21, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> Fitzgerald, Boldin, and [[Steve Breaston]], who filled in for the injured Boldin, became the fifth 1,000 yard receiving trio in NFL history.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Collette |first=Christopher |date=January 27, 2009 |title=Cardinals' trio of receivers far from anonymous |url=https://www.wtsp.com/article/news/cardinals-trio-of-receivers-far-from-anonymous/67-391729813 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230422170646/https://www.wtsp.com/article/news/cardinals-trio-of-receivers-far-from-anonymous/67-391729813 |archive-date=April 22, 2023 |access-date=April 21, 2023 |website=WTSP |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Baltimore Ravens===

====2010 season====
[[File:Anquan Boldin with US Army soldiers in 2010.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Boldin (center) with service members of the [[United States Armed Forces|US Armed Forces]] while with the Ravens in 2010 at McDaniel College]] 
On March 5, 2010, Boldin was traded to the Baltimore Ravens for the Ravens third and fourth-round picks in the [[2010 NFL draft]]. The Ravens also received a fifth-round pick from the Cardinals as part of the deal.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 5, 2010 |title=Cardinals trade Boldin to Ravens for draft picks |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=4970057 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210908122702/https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=4970057 |archive-date=September 8, 2021 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=ESPN.com |language=en |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> Boldin agreed to a three-year deal worth $25 million, in addition to the one year he had left on his then-current deal, bringing the total deal to $28 million over four years, with $10 million guaranteed.<ref name="Boldin traded to Ravens">{{Cite web |last=Urban |first=Darren |date=March 5, 2010 |title=Boldin Era Ends With Trade |url=https://www.azcardinals.com/news/boldin-era-ends-with-trade-1095711 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221201134414/https://www.azcardinals.com/news/boldin-era-ends-with-trade-1095711 |archive-date=December 1, 2022 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=Arizona Cardinals |language=en-US}}</ref>

In Boldin's Week 1 debut as a Raven, he caught seven passes for 110 yards, and was one of the few offensive players with strong contributions in the 10–9 defensive game eventually won over the [[2010 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] by Baltimore.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Baltimore Ravens at New York Jets – September 13th, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201009130nyj.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171231155350/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201009130nyj.htm |archive-date=December 31, 2017 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In Week 3, against the division rival [[2010 Cleveland Browns season|Cleveland Browns]], Boldin caught eight passes for 142 yards and three touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cleveland Browns at Baltimore Ravens – September 26th, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201009260rav.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171231051721/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201009260rav.htm |archive-date=December 31, 2017 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He became the fastest player in NFL history to reach 600 receptions, doing so in just 98 games.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 26, 2010 |title=Anquan Boldin Makes History |url=http://www.footballnewsnow.com/2010/anquan-boldin-makes-history/ |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721150728/http://www.footballnewsnow.com/2010/anquan-boldin-makes-history/ |archive-date=July 21, 2011 |access-date=December 28, 2010 |website=Football News Now}}. Football News Now. Retrieved on February 4, 2013.</ref> Boldin won AFC Offensive Player of the Week honors for his performance.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hensley |first=Jamison |date=September 29, 2010 |title=Boldin shrugs off AFC offensive player of the week award |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/bs-mtblog-2010-09-boldin_shrugs_off_afc_offensive_player_of_the_week_award-story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711000722/https://www.baltimoresun.com/bs-mtblog-2010-09-boldin_shrugs_off_afc_offensive_player_of_the_week_award-story.html |archive-date=July 11, 2021 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=Baltimore Sun}} Retrieved August 18, 2012.</ref> The Ravens faced their arch-rivals, the [[2010 Pittsburgh Steelers season|Pittsburgh Steelers]], in Week 13 on [[NBC Sunday Night Football|Sunday Night Football]]. Boldin was the game's leading receiver with five catches, 118 yards, a 61-yard catch and a touchdown in Baltimore's 13–10 loss.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pittsburgh Steelers at Baltimore Ravens – December 5th, 2010 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201012050rav.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322231907/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201012050rav.htm |archive-date=March 22, 2019 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

In his first season with the Ravens, Boldin recorded 64 receptions for 837 yards and seven touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anquan Boldin 2010 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BoldAn00/gamelog/2010/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201002211142/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BoldAn00/gamelog/2010/ |archive-date=October 2, 2020 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

In the [[2010–11 NFL playoffs#AFC: Baltimore Ravens 30, Kansas City Chiefs 7|Wild Card Round]] of the playoffs, the Ravens took on the [[2010 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]]. Boldin caught five passes for 64 yards and a touchdown in the 30–7 rout.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wild Card – Baltimore Ravens at Kansas City Chiefs – January 9th, 2011 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201101090kan.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121129064620/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201101090kan.htm |archive-date=November 29, 2012 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> The following week, Boldin would only record one reception for −2 yards as the Ravens had their season ended in the [[2010–11 NFL playoffs#AFC: Pittsburgh Steelers 31, Baltimore Ravens 24|Divisional Round]] with another loss to the Steelers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Divisional Round – Baltimore Ravens at Pittsburgh Steelers – January 15th, 2011 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201101150pit.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171110080414/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201101150pit.htm |archive-date=November 10, 2017 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

====2011 season====
Boldin had eight catches for 132 yards in a Week 6 victory over the [[2011 Houston Texans season|Houston Texans]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Houston Texans at Baltimore Ravens – October 16th, 2011 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201110160rav.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170702194524/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201110160rav.htm |archive-date=July 2, 2017 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He continued his strong level of play the following week, catching seven passes for a season-high 145 yards as he helped the Ravens put together their biggest comeback win ever against his former team, the [[2011 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arizona Cardinals at Baltimore Ravens – October 30th, 2011 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201110300rav.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221011170126/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201110300rav.htm |archive-date=October 11, 2022 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

Boldin finished the regular season as the Ravens leading receiver once again, catching 57 passes for 887 yards, topping his total from 2010, but also had four fewer touchdowns, only scoring three on the year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2011 Baltimore Ravens Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees, Injury Reports |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/rav/2011.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171231155353/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/rav/2011.htm |archive-date=December 31, 2017 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Anquan Boldin 2011 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BoldAn00/gamelog/2011/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201002211144/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BoldAn00/gamelog/2011/ |archive-date=October 2, 2020 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

In the [[2011–12 NFL playoffs#AFC: Baltimore Ravens 20, Houston Texans 13|Divisional Round]], Boldin and the Ravens faced the Texans once again. He had four catches for 73 yards and a touchdown. He also caught a much-needed pass on the sideline with one hand. The Ravens would win 20–13 and move on to the [[AFC Championship Game]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Divisional Round – Houston Texans at Baltimore Ravens – January 15th, 2012 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201201150rav.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171231155413/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201201150rav.htm |archive-date=December 31, 2017 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

===San Francisco 49ers===

====2013 season====
On March 11, 2013, Boldin was traded to the [[San Francisco 49ers]] for a sixth-round pick in the [[2013 NFL draft]].<ref name="Boldin49ers">{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Aaron  |date=March 11, 2013 |title=Anquan Boldin traded to 49ers for sixth-round draft pick, sources say |url=http://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/ravens/ravens-insider/bal-sources-anquan-boldin-traded-to-49ers-for-sixthround-draft-pick-20130311,0,7576464.story |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130312005412/http://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/ravens/ravens-insider/bal-sources-anquan-boldin-traded-to-49ers-for-sixthround-draft-pick-20130311,0,7576464.story |archive-date=March 12, 2013 |access-date=March 11, 2013 |website=[[The Baltimore Sun]]}}</ref>
On September 8, 2013, in the season opener against the [[2013 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]] which was also his debut game as a 49er, the 49ers defeated the Packers 34–28. Boldin racked up 208 yards and a touchdown on 13 receptions during that game.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Price |first=Taylor |date=September 8, 2013 |title=Anquan Boldin Posts 208-Yard Debut |url=http://www.49ers.com/news/article-2/Anquan-Boldin-Posts-208-Yard-Debut/582bf421-0ca4-4005-97de-40d5acdd092a |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160822091653/http://www.49ers.com/news/article-2/Anquan-Boldin-Posts-208-Yard-Debut/582bf421-0ca4-4005-97de-40d5acdd092a |archive-date=August 22, 2016 |access-date=July 28, 2016 |website=San Francisco 49ers}}</ref> His Week 1 performance earned him NFC Offensive Player of the Week.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2013 NFL Week 1 Leaders & Scores |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2013/week_1.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210928155528/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2013/week_1.htm |archive-date=September 28, 2021 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He became the first wide receiver to ever gain over 100 yards for three different teams on his team debut. Boldin closed out the regular season with nine receptions for 149 receiving yards and one receiving touchdown in the 23–20 victory over the [[2013 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=San Francisco 49ers at Arizona Cardinals – December 29th, 2013 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201312290crd.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170901070824/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201312290crd.htm |archive-date=September 1, 2017 |access-date=April 21, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> Boldin finished his first year with the 49ers with 85 receptions and 1,179 yards as well as seven touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anquan Boldin 2013 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BoldAn00/gamelog/2013/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201002211149/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BoldAn00/gamelog/2013/ |archive-date=October 2, 2020 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He won the NFLPA Alan Page Community Award.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFLPA Alan Page Community Award Winners |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/awards/nflpa-alan-page-community-award.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927215254/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/awards/nflpa-alan-page-community-award.htm |archive-date=September 27, 2022 |access-date=April 21, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

In the [[2013–14 NFL playoffs#NFC: San Francisco 49ers 23, Carolina Panthers 10|Divisional Round]] of the playoffs against the [[2013 Carolina Panthers season|Carolina Panthers]], Boldin had eight receptions for 136 receiving yards in the 23–10 victory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Divisional Round – San Francisco 49ers at Carolina Panthers – January 12th, 2014 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201401120car.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190321140243/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201401120car.htm |archive-date=March 21, 2019 |access-date=April 21, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> In the [[2013–14 NFL playoffs#NFC: Seattle Seahawks 23, San Francisco 49ers 17|NFC Championship]] against the [[2013 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]], he had a receiving touchdown in the 23–17 loss.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFC Championship – San Francisco 49ers at Seattle Seahawks – January 19th, 2014 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201401190sea.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804014329/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201401190sea.htm |archive-date=August 4, 2017 |access-date=April 21, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Buffalo Bills and retirement===
On August 7, 2017, Boldin signed a one-year contract with the [[Buffalo Bills]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Orr |first=Conor |date=August 7, 2017 |title=Anquan Boldin signs one-year deal with Buffalo Bills |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/anquan-boldin-signs-one-year-deal-with-buffalo-bills-0ap3000000826632 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170808080348/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000826632/article/anquan-boldin-signing-oneyear-deal-with-buffalo-bills |archive-date=August 8, 2017 |access-date=August 7, 2017 |website=NFL.com}}</ref> He appeared in a preseason loss to the Eagles, catching one pass for five yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anquan Boldin game logs |work=The Football Database |url=https://www.footballdb.com/players/anquan-boldin-boldian01/gamelogs |access-date=July 21, 2025}}</ref> On August 20, less than two weeks after joining the team, Boldin abruptly retired, saying "his life's purpose is bigger than football" and he intended to focus on humanitarian work.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Patra |first=Kevin |date=August 20, 2017 |title=Veteran WR Anquan Boldin retires after 14 seasons |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/veteran-wr-anquan-boldin-retires-after-14-seasons-0ap3000000832739 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170821130017/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000832739/article/veteran-wr-anquan-boldin-retires-after-14-seasons |archive-date=August 21, 2017 |access-date=August 21, 2017 |website=NFL.com}}</ref>

An official retirement ceremony for Boldin took place with the Baltimore Ravens on October 14, 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Walker |first=Childs |date=October 14, 2019 |title=Anquan Boldin, remembered for Super Bowl heroics and 'huge' presence in locker room, community, retires as a Raven |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/ravens/bs-sp-ravens-anquan-boldin-retire-20191014-qzakirrj3zecxokefwmkw6r5zq-story.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211016121307/https://www.baltimoresun.com/sports/ravens/bs-sp-ravens-anquan-boldin-retire-20191014-qzakirrj3zecxokefwmkw6r5zq-story.html |archive-date=October 16, 2021 |access-date=April 20, 2023 |website=[[The Baltimore Sun]]}}</ref>

'''Angelo Delvonne Crowell''' (born August 16, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Buffalo Bills]] in the third round of the [[2003 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2003 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2003/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Virginia Cavaliers football|Virginia Cavaliers]].

He is the younger brother of former NFL [[wide receiver]] [[Germane Crowell]].

==College career==
Crowell attended the [[University of Virginia]], where he served as co-captain in 2002. Received 1st Team All-ACC honors in 2002. Set a school record for tackles of 144 in 2001, and then broke his own record the following year.

===Buffalo Bills===
He served primarily as a reserve linebacker for his first two seasons, playing only on special teams.  In 2005, after [[Takeo Spikes]] went down with a season ending tear of the Achilles tendon Crowell took a spot on the starting roster.  He went on that season to record 119 tackles, 1 forced fumble, and 2 interceptions in 12 starts.

In the summer of 2006, he was named the starting strong side linebacker by Buffalo head coach [[Dick Jauron]], replacing [[Jeff Posey]]. Crowell started every game until suffering a late season injury against the [[San Diego Chargers]].

Crowell underwent arm surgery after tearing his [[triceps]] muscle in the final game of the 2007 season.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.buffalobills.com/news/news.jsp?NEWS_ID=5998 |title=Catching Up With Crowell |access-date=April 17, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080421001113/http://www.buffalobills.com/news/news.jsp?NEWS_ID=5998 |archive-date=April 21, 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On September 4, 2008, Crowell was placed on season-ending [[injured reserve]] after undergoing knee surgery.

===Tampa Bay Buccaneers===
An [[unrestricted free agent]] after the 2008 season, Crowell signed with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] on March 18, 2009.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20090322163336/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2009/football/nfl/wires/03/18/2020.ap.fbn.buccaneers.crowell.0194/index.html Bucs Sign Crowell] SI.com, March 19, 2009</ref> He was placed on season-ending injured reserve on August 24 after suffering a torn [[Biceps brachii muscle|biceps muscle]] during the preseason. On June 18, 2010, Crowell was released by the Buccaneers.

===Omaha Nighthawks===
Crowell was signed by the [[Omaha Nighthawks]] of the [[United Football League (2009–)|United Football League]] on August 23, 2011.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oursportscentral.com/services/releases/?id=4281147 |title=UFL Transactions |date=August 23, 2010 |work=OurSports Central |accessdate=August 27, 2011}}</ref>

'''Andrew Warren Katzenmoyer''' (born December 2, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for the [[New England Patriots]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the Patriots in the first round (28th overall) of the [[1999 NFL draft]] and won [[Super Bowl XXXVI]] with the team, though he did not play a game that season. He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]], and became the first Buckeye to win the [[Butkus Award]]. His playing career was shortened due to a neck injury.

==Early life==
Katzenmoyer was born in [[Kettering, Ohio]]. He and his family moved to [[Westerville, Ohio]] when he was 5. He attended [[Westerville South High School]], and played [[high school football]] for the Westerville South Wildcats. Katzenmoyer won the 1995 [[Associated Press]] [[Mr. Football (Ohio)|Mr. Football Award]] for the state of Ohio,<ref>{{cite news|title=Katzenmoyer is Mr. Football|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-recorder/181246133/|newspaper=The Times Recorder|page=21|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 30, 1995|access-date=September 17, 2025}}{{Open access}}</ref> and was named the 1995 ''[[USA Today]]'' [[USA Today All-USA High School Football Team|All-USA Team]] Defensive Player of the Year.<ref>{{cite news|title=USA Today All-USA Team|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/usa-today/181245799/|newspaper=USA Today|page=24|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 26, 1995|access-date=September 17, 2025}}{{Open access}}</ref>

The Wildcats football team was state of Ohio [[List of OHSAA football champions|high school championship]] runner-ups in his junior year (1994).<ref>{{cite news|title=St. Ignatius rolls to 4th title in a row (Part 1)|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-plain-dealer/181247169/|newspaper=The Plain Dealer|first=Eddie|last=Dwyer|page=53|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 4, 1994|access-date=September 17, 2025}}{{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=St. Ignatius rolls to 4th title in a row (Part 2)|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-plain-dealer/181247305/|newspaper=The Plain Dealer|first=Eddie|last=Dwyer|page=69|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 4, 1994|access-date=September 17, 2025}}{{Open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=St. Ignatius defense gets a jump-start|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-plain-dealer/181247332/|newspaper=The Plain Dealer|first=Eddie|last=Dwyer|page=69|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 4, 1994|access-date=September 17, 2025}}{{Open access}}</ref> In his senior year (1995), the Wildcats were ranked nationally at #14 in the ''[[USA Today]]'' Super 25,<ref>{{cite news|title=USA Today Super 25|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/usa-today/181248475/|newspaper=USA Today|page=13|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 14, 1995|access-date=September 17, 2025}}{{Open access}}</ref> and were 11–0 before losing to [[Boardman High School|Youngstown Boardman]] in the regional finals.<ref>{{cite news|title=Area teams bounce back in big way|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-cincinnati-enquirer/181248619/|newspaper=Cincinnati Enquirer\first=Dave|last=Schutte|page=42|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 19, 1995|access-date=September 17, 2025}}{{Open access}}</ref>

==College career==
Katzenmoyer attended Ohio State University, where he played for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football]] team from 1996 to 1998.  In the first game of his college career, he became the first true freshman to ever start at linebacker for the Buckeyes. As a freshman  he recorded 12 sacks including three in the [[1997 Rose Bowl]].<ref name=nack11251996>William Nack, "[https://web.archive.org/web/20090926015621/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1009100/index.htm Born to be a Buckeye]," ''Sports Illustrated'' (November 25, 1996). Retrieved February 2, 2012.</ref> As a sophomore in 1997, he was recognized as a consensus first-team All-American, and won the [[Dick Butkus Award]] and [[Lambert Award|Jack Lambert Trophy]]. Katzenmoyer was a three time first-team all-Big Ten selection. He started 37 consecutive games and finished his college career with 256 tackles, 50 tackles-for-loss, 18 sacks and six Interceptions. In 2009, he was inducted into the Ohio State Athletics Hall Of Fame.{{citation needed|date=September 2016}} Notably, he was the last player at Ohio State to wear number 45.

==Professional career==
The [[New England Patriots]] selected Katzenmoyer in the first round (28th pick overall) of the [[1999 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1999 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1999/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

In Week 6 of the [[1999 New England Patriots season|1999 season]], Katzenmoyer became the second rookie in NFL history to record 2.0+ sacks and a touchdown in a single game, the first being [[Todd Shell]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Farrar |first=Doug |title=Seahawks rookie CB Devon Witherspoon makes NFL history with massive game |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2023/10/02/seahawks-rookie-cb-devon-witherspoon-makes-nfl-history-with-massive-game/71040339007/ |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref> He had intercepted a pass from [[1999 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]] quarterback [[Dan Marino]] in the first three minutes of the first quarter, and returned it for 57 yards. As of 2023, only 1 other rookie, [[Devon Witherspoon]], had achieved this statistic afterwards.

He suffered a neck injury during his first season with the Patriots. After playing in 24 games with 14 starts throughout his career, he was eventually forced to have surgery and miss half of the [[2000 New England Patriots season|2000 season]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Felder |first=Michael |date=June 7, 2018 |title=Whatever Happened To: Andy Katzenmoyer, the Big Kat |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1124686-whatever-happened-to-andy-katzenmoyer-the-big-kat |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}}</ref> During [[National Football League Training Camp|training camp]] in 2001, Katzenmoyer walked out, citing concern about a feeling in his neck.  He was placed on [[injured reserve]] for the entire [[2001 New England Patriots season|2001 season]].

On June 14, 2002, the Patriots released Katzenmoyer.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Patriots release LB Andy Katzenmoyer |url=https://www.patriots.com/news/patriots-release-lb-andy-katzenmoyer-149756 |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=www.patriots.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Katzenmoyer is now a risk management adviser for Hosket Ulen Insurance Solutions along with serving on the board for neighborhood bridges.

'''Anthony''' "'''Spice'''" '''Adams''' (born June 18, 1980) is an American television host, actor, comedian, and former professional [[American football|football]] player. He played as a [[defensive tackle]] for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). After playing [[college football]] for the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State Nittany Lions]], Adams was selected by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in the second round of the [[2003 NFL draft]], for whom he played four seasons, followed by the [[Chicago Bears]] from 2007 to 2011.

After his football career, Adams became involved in social media and television. He is a former co-host of ''[[The Great American Baking Show]]'', the American adaptation of ''[[The Great British Bake Off]]''.

==Early life and college==
Adams attended [[Martin Luther King Jr. Senior High School]] in [[Detroit]], [[Michigan]], and [[Pennsylvania State University]]. He played for the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football]] team from 1999 to 2002, being named to the academic all-[[Big Ten Conference]] team and honorable mention all-Big Ten.<ref name="Top 50">{{cite web|last=Rice|first=Jeff|url=https://247sports.com/college/penn-state/Article/Former-Penn-State-defensive-tackle-Anthony-Adams-brought-spice-and-skills-to-squad-46255902/|title=Top 50 of 2000s: No. 25|publisher=[[247Sports]]|date=July 15, 2016|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

During his freshman year, he recorded four tackles in nine games, which increased to 36 tackles and a sack the following season. As a junior, he had 59 tackles, 3.5 sacks, and led the team in tackles-for-loss with 11. In his senior year, he had 67 tackles, two sacks, 13 tackles-for-loss, and four pass breakups.<ref name="Top 50" /> The 2002 Nittany Lions entered the [[2003 Capital One Bowl]] with the chance to record their first top-ten ranking since 1996, but lost to [[Auburn Tigers football|Auburn]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Rudel|first=Neil|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/37002028/|title=Lions take huge step back|newspaper=[[Public Opinion (Chambersburg)|Public Opinion]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=January 2, 2003|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

Adams graduated with a business degree in 2003.<ref>{{cite web|last=Pryor|first=Maddy|url=https://news.psu.edu/story/494625/2017/11/15/athletics/comedy-helping-former-nittany-lion-make-name-himself-outside|title=Comedy helping former Nittany Lion make a name for himself outside of football|publisher=Penn State News|date=November 15, 2017|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

===San Francisco 49ers===
The [[San Francisco 49ers]] selected Adams in the second round (57th overall) of the [[2003 NFL draft]];<ref>{{Cite web |title=2003 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2003/draft.htm |access-date=March 28, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> the 49ers, who lost two starting defensive linemen during the offseason, drafted Adams and defensive end [[Andrew Williams (American football)|Andrew Williams]] in the following round to fill the gap.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/36999687/|title=Harris slips down to happy Niners|agency=[[Associated Press|AP]]|newspaper=Tulare Advance-Register|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=April 28, 2003|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

[[File:Anthony Adams and Jamar Williams.jpg|thumb|left|150px|Adams and [[Jamar Williams]] taking the field in 2009]]

Adams became a free agent after the 2006 season, ending his 49ers tenure with 155 tackles and six sacks in 58 games.

===Chicago Bears===
On March 25, 2007, he signed a four-year contract with the [[Chicago Bears]]; team writer Larry Mayer described Adams as "an undersized but quick tackle who seemingly is an ideal fit for the Bears' one-gap defense."<ref>{{cite web|last=Mayer|first=Larry|url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/NewsStory.asp?story_id=3211|title=Bears ink free agent Adams|publisher=[[Chicago Bears]]|date=March 25, 2007|access-date=October 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070331195841/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/NewsStory.asp?story_id=3211|archive-date=March 31, 2007}}</ref> In 2010, he started all 16 games and the Bears' playoff games; at season's end, he was named a [[Brian Piccolo Award]] recipient. The following season, he only started four games and appeared in 11, and was released on February 26, 2012.<ref>{{cite web|last=Florio|first=Mike|url=https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2012/02/26/bears-bounce-anthony-adams/|title=Bears bounce Anthony Adams|publisher=[[Profootballtalk.com]]|date=February 26, 2012|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

He announced his retirement via [[YouTube]] on March 24, 2013.<ref>{{cite web|author=Inman, Cam|url=http://www.mercurynews.com/sports/ci_22861237/former-49ers-lineman-anthony-adams-retires-via-youtube|title=Former 49ers lineman Anthony Adams retires via YouTube|work=San Jose Mercury News|date=March 25, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Jensen |first=Sean |url=http://blogs.suntimes.com/bears/2013/03/anthony_adams_files_retirement.html |title=Anthony Adams files retirement papers |newspaper=[[Chicago Sun-Times]] |date=March 23, 2013 |access-date=March 23, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130325102014/http://blogs.suntimes.com/bears/2013/03/anthony_adams_files_retirement.html |archive-date=March 25, 2013 }}</ref> In nine seasons, he served primarily as a depth player, starting at least eight games in three years.<ref>{{cite web|last=Pompei|first=Dan|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/970250/2019/05/12/how-former-bears-nfl-role-player-anthony-spice-adams-became-a-social-media-sensation/|title=How former NFL role player Anthony 'Spice' Adams became a social media sensation|publisher=[[The Athletic]]|date=May 12, 2019|access-date=October 10, 2019}} {{subscription required}}</ref> He ended his career with 278 tackles and 10.5 sacks.<ref>{{cite news|last=Hockensmith|first=Dan|url=https://www.pennlive.com/pennstatefootball/2013/08/former_penn_state_dt_anthony_s.html|title=Former Penn State DT Anthony 'Spice' Adams releases second parody video about pork|newspaper=[[The Patriot-News]]|date=August 26, 2013|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Adams and his wife, Andenika, have four children. Teammates have bestowed several nicknames on Adams: Former 49ers teammate [[Bryant Young]] dubbed him "Double A" not only for his initials but also for his suspicion that Adams' extra energy came from batteries. His Penn State teammates nicknamed him "Spice".<ref name=haugh/> Adams was voted "Mama's Boy" his senior year at [[Martin Luther King High School (Detroit)|Martin Luther King High School]] in Detroit.<ref name=haugh/> He is a member of [[Omega Psi Phi]] fraternity and was initiated at Nu chapter. In the summer of 2012, Adams produced a series of videos on [[YouTube]] about life as an NFL free agent.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GoXw17yIevI | title = Stuff NFL Free Agents Say| website = [[YouTube]]}}</ref>  On May 5, 2013, Adams earned his master's degree in Business Administration from George Washington University.

===Community involvement===
Since 2006, Adams has been involved with Youthville, a program in his hometown of Detroit. He gave away two [[Super Bowl XL]] tickets to the student who demonstrated the greatest improvement in [[Grading in education|grade point average]]. In 2009, Adams visited several [[Chicago Public Schools]] to help students write letters to troops overseas during the [[Iraq War|Iraq]] and [[War in Afghanistan (2001–present)|Afghanistan]] wars.

==Media career==
During his tenure with the 49ers, Adams was a blogger and hosted an online show with teammate [[Mike Adams (safety)|Mike Adams]] called ''The Adams Report''.<ref name=haugh>{{cite news|last=Haugh|first=David|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-2007-11-11-0711100527-story.html|title=Women in his life gems, solid as rocks|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]|date=November 11, 2007|access-date=October 10, 2019}}</ref>

Starting on September 14, 2013, Adams began hosting a weekly half-hour show titled ''Inside the Bears'', which airs on [[WFLD]] and [[WPWR-TV]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Former-Bear-Anthony-Adams-hosting-new-magazine-show/754b0a0d-888b-476e-bb72-67dd14294771 |title=Former Bear Anthony Adams hosting new magazine show |last=Mayer |first=Larry |date=July 17, 2013 |publisher=[[Chicago Bears]] |access-date=July 17, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130721054209/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Former-Bear-Anthony-Adams-hosting-new-magazine-show/754b0a0d-888b-476e-bb72-67dd14294771 |archive-date=July 21, 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2016, Adams began a recurring role on the [[HBO]] series ''[[Ballers]]''. He was announced on September 21, 2017, as one of the new hosts of ''[[The Great American Baking Show]]'', an American adaptation of ''[[The Great British Bake Off]]'', on [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Barney|first1=Chuck|title=Ayesha Curry lands another big TV gig — this time with ABC|url=http://www.mercurynews.com/2017/09/21/ayesha-curry-lands-another-big-tv-gig-this-time-with-abc/|access-date=October 13, 2017|work=The Mercury News|publisher=Bay Area News Group|date=September 21, 2017|quote=Curry, the wife of Golden State Warriors all-star Steph Curry, will host the third season of the show along with former San Francisco 49er Anthony 'Spice' Adams.}}</ref>

Adams is well known for his [[Instagram]] account, where he posts comedic videos under the username "spiceadams". Many of the characters and skits he has created have gone viral since 2018; an example is his catchphrase "ahaha", which became the subject of multiple memes on [[Twitter]], and a photo of him hiding behind a tree in a bright yellow suit while rubbing his hands together and licking his lips in an expression of desire for what he is looking at.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/24/sports/football/anthony-spice-adams-ahaha.html|title=Memes Made Spice Adams More Famous Than the N.F.L. Could|newspaper=The New York Times|date=October 24, 2019|last1=Goble|first1=Corban}}</ref>

'''Anthony Carter''' (born September 17, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for 13 years in the [[United States Football League]] (USFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL). He made three-consecutive [[Pro Bowls]] for the [[Minnesota Vikings]] and was honored by Minnesota as one of the 50 Greatest Vikings of all time.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.vikings.com/team/legends/50-greatest-vikings|title=50 Greatest Vikings|publisher=Minnesota Vikings}}</ref> Carter played [[college football]] for the [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan Wolverines]], finishing his career as a three-time [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]], and a two-time [[List of unanimous All-Americans in college football|unanimous All-American]] selection. He is currently third all-time in receiving yards, and second all-time in receiving touchdowns for the [[University of Michigan]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Michigan Wolverines Receiving Stats |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/michigan/receiving.html |access-date=2024-10-12 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

==College career==
Carter played at the [[University of Michigan]] from 1979 to 1982. Although the Wolverines employed an offense that relied mostly on its [[running back]]s, he was one of the most productive receivers in the school's history. Standing 5 feet, 11 inches tall and weighing only 160 pounds, Carter relied on his speed to make plays and provided an effective counterpoint to coach [[Bo Schembechler]]'s running game plan. In addition to his duties as a receiver, he was also the team's kickoff and punt returner for most of his career. Carter caught more than two passes in a game only once that season, but made the most of it when the ball was thrown to him with 7-of-17 receptions accounting for [[touchdown]]s. He averaged 27.2 yards per catch.

His 45-yard TD catch and run against [[Indiana Hoosiers football|Indiana]] as time ran out to give Michigan a 27–21 victory is considered one of the greatest plays in [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan football]] history, and the radio call by the legendary [[Bob Ufer]] is also considered a classic. In that game, [[Lee Corso]]'s Indiana Hoosiers had tied it up with about a minute to go. At that time, college games could end in a tie, and Michigan had a 6–1 overall record, 4–0 in the Big Ten. While a tie was essentially as good as a win from Indiana's perspective, a tie was as good as a loss from Michigan's perspective. On the ensuing drive, Michigan was only able to get to the Indiana 45-yard line with time fast running out. Things looked grim, but with six seconds remaining, Carter told quarterback John Wangler in the huddle, "Hey, Johnny. Throw the ball to me. I'm going to be open." On the next play, Carter, sprinting left to right, met Wangler's pass in a seam over the middle at the Hoosier 25. He made a one-step cutback to his left to avoid one tackle and slipped another tackle at the 5-yard line before bounding into the endzone after time had expired.

By his sophomore year, Carter was the Wolverines primary option at receiver. That season, he became the first sophomore to be voted Michigan team [[Most Valuable Player|MVP]]. As a three-time [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]], he was named [[Big Ten Most Valuable Player]] his senior season, and finished fourth in voting for the [[Heisman Trophy]]. He was the third NCAA Division I FBS athlete to total 1,000 career yards on both [[kick return]]s and [[punt return]]s. He holds the NCAA career record for highest average gain per play (Min. 5,000 yards, 275-374 plays, 5,197 on 298).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://web1.ncaa.org/web_files/stats/football_records/DI/2009/2009FBS.pdf |title=2009 Division I Football Records Book: Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) Records |access-date=2010-07-09 |publisher=[[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] |page=21}}</ref>

In 2001, Carter was elected to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]]. On December 12, 2014, the [[Big Ten Network]] included Carter on "The Mount Rushmore of [[University of Michigan Football|Michigan Football]]", as chosen by online fan voting. Carter was joined in the honor by [[Charles Woodson]], [[Tom Harmon]], and [[Desmond Howard]].

===Records===
When he graduated, Carter held nearly every Michigan career receiving and return record. He was the school's all-time leader in:

* touchdowns: 40 (now ranks fifth; record held by [[Anthony Thomas (American football)|Anthony Thomas]] with 55)
* receptions: 161 (now ranks fifth; record held by [[Braylon Edwards]] with 252)
* receiving yards: 3,076 (now ranks second; record held by Braylon Edwards with 3,541)
* touchdown receptions: 37 (now ranks second; record held by Braylon Edwards with 39)
* punt returns: 79 (now ranks second; record held by [[Steve Breaston]] with 127)
* punt return yardage: 907 (now ranks second; record held by Steve Breaston with 1,599)
* kickoff returns: 63 (now ranks second; record held by Steve Breaston with 81)
* kickoff return yardage: 1,606 (now ranks second; record held by Steve Breaston with 1,993)

His average of 17.4 yards-per-play was an [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] record.

==Professional career==

===USFL===

Upon graduating from college, Anthony Carter chose to play in the upstart [[United States Football League|USFL]], rather than in the NFL. The league employed a territorial draft, aimed at sending players to teams whose fans were already familiar with them. Because of this unique system, the [[Michigan Panthers]] were allowed to select Carter prior to the league's traditional draft.

1983 was Carter's first season with the Panthers and one of his most successful as a professional. Although the team started 1–4, they finished the regular season 12-6 and went on to defeat the [[Philadelphia/Baltimore Stars|Philadelphia Stars]] to win the first USFL championship. With his team behind late in the fourth quarter, he scored the game-winning touchdown on a 48-yard pass from [[Bobby Hebert]]. He finished the game with nine receptions for 179 yards. For the season, he gained 1,081 yards on 60 catches, nine of them touchdowns.

Carter's 1984 season was cut short after only six games when his arm was broken in a game against the [[San Antonio Gunslingers (USFL team)|San Antonio Gunslingers]]. Before the 1985 season the Panthers merged with the [[Oakland Invaders]]. In his last USFL season, he led his team in receiving yards (1,323), receptions (70), and receiving touchdowns (14) and was named 2nd Team All-USFL and made the Sporting News' All-USFL team.

===NFL===
After the 1985 USFL season, Carter signed with the NFL's [[Miami Dolphins]], who drafted Carter back in 1983 in order to secure his NFL rights. However, he was traded to the [[Minnesota Vikings]] before playing a game with the team. He led the Vikings in receptions five of his first six seasons with the team, and was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] in 1987, 1988, and 1989. In the 1987 season, Carter helped his team reach the NFC championship. He set an NFL playoff record (since surpassed) with 143 punt return yards in their wildcard win over the [[New Orleans Saints]], and caught 10 receptions for a then NFL playoff record 227 yards, along with 1 carry for 30 yards and two punt returns for 21 in the Vikings 36–24 upset win over the 13-2 [[San Francisco 49ers]] in the divisional playoff round. The 642 all purpose yards he gained in the 1987 playoffs remain a single postseason record.

The following season, he caught 4 passes for 102 yards in a 28-17 wild card round win over the [[Los Angeles Rams]]. Although [[Cris Carter]] became the team's number one receiver in 1991, Anthony Carter remained an effective offensive weapon through 1993, his final season with the team.

The final two years of Carter's pro career were spent in the same state where it began, this time with the [[Detroit Lions]]. Most of his time with the Lions was spent attempting to come back from injury. He played in only four games in 1994, and failed to catch a pass in 1995.

Carter finished his 11 NFL seasons with 486 receptions for 7,733 yards and 55 touchdowns. He also rushed for 289 yards and 2 touchdowns, returned 15 punts for 165 yards, and returned 4 kickoffs for 65 yards.

'''Andrew Paul Lee''' (born August 11, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[punter (gridiron football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Pittsburgh Panthers football|Pittsburgh Panthers]], and was selected by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in the sixth round of the [[2004 NFL draft]]. Lee also played for the [[Cleveland Browns]], [[Carolina Panthers]], and [[Arizona Cardinals]]. He was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] following the 2007, 2009, and 2011 seasons.

==Early life==
Lee was born in [[Westminster, South Carolina]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dorsett |first=Chad |date=April 17, 2013 |title=Andy Lee remembering Westminster Rec |url=https://wsnwradio.com/andy-lee-remembering-westminster-rec/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=94.1 – The Lake / WSNW |language=en-US}}</ref> He graduated from [[West-Oak High School]] in Westminster.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kroichick |first=Ron  |date=December 7, 2011 |title=Punter Andy Lee gives 49ers a leg up |url=https://www.sfgate.com/sports/article/Punter-Andy-Lee-gives-49ers-a-leg-up-2354340.php |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=SFGATE}}</ref> At West-Oak High School, Lee was a three-sport star athlete, lettering in football, baseball, and basketball. In football, he punted and played tight end and wide receiver as a senior. His punting average as a senior was 42.8 yards, earning him a 33rd ranking in [[South Carolina]] by SuperPrep. Lee was selected twice to All-Conference honors in basketball and helped lead the baseball team to a district championship and the state playoffs. As a pitcher, he went 5–0 as a junior and 8–2 as a senior, with a selection to the North-South Baseball All-Star Game and a Golden and Silver Arm Award.{{citation needed|date=August 2023}}

==College career==
Lee attended the [[University of Pittsburgh]] and played for the [[Pittsburgh Panthers football]] team from 2000 to 2003.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/andy-lee-1.html |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He was Pittsburgh's starting punter for three seasons after winning the starting role late in true freshman season (2000). His 244 punts and 10,353 yards are tops in school history.<ref name="Pitt">{{Cite web |date=20 May 2008 |title=Where Are They Now - Andy Lee |url=https://pittsburghpanthers.com/news/2008/5/20/Where_Are_They_Now_Andy_Lee |access-date=15 September 2024 |website=Pitt Panthers |language=en |archive-date=September 15, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240915053351/https://pittsburghpanthers.com/news/2008/5/20/Where_Are_They_Now_Andy_Lee |url-status=live }}</ref> Lee had 29 fair catches, 61 kicks downed inside 20-yard line and three blocked kicks.{{citation needed|date=August 2023}} He was the only player to ever win [[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East Conference]] Special Teams Player of the Year honors twice in career.<ref name="Pitt" /> As a senior, Lee was a semi-finalist for the [[Ray Guy Award]], given to college football's top punter.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 27, 2003 |title=Ray
