===San Francisco 49ers===
====2004 season====
Following a successful collegiate career, Lee was selected in the sixth round of the NFL Draft with the 188th overall pick by the [[San Francisco 49ers]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |archive-date=November 1, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181101231250/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Lee had never attended an NFL game growing up in South Carolina. Even when he went on to become a standout punter on the collegiate level at the University of Pittsburgh, he was still a stranger to live NFL action.
In Lee's rookie season, he punted 96 times with 25 dropped inside the 20 and an NFL-long of 81 yards.
His punting average of 41.6 yards per punt was first time a 49ers punter averaged over 40 yards per punt since [[Reggie Roby]] in 1998. Lee also posted seven punts for 338 yards (48.3 avg.), including career-long of 81 yards with one punt downed inside 20-yard line at Tampa Bay (11–21). His 81-yarder was fourth-longest in 49ers history and NFL's longest punt of the year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2004 NFL Leaders and Leaderboards |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/leaders.htm |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |archive-date=May 15, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210515042330/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/leaders.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

====2005 season====
In 2005, Lee set a career-high with 107 punts (41.6 avg.), including 15 punts downed inside the 20. His three touchbacks in 107 punts was third-best ratio of touchbacks-to-punts among punters with 30 or more kicks in 2005, trailing [[Houston Texans|Houston]]’s  [[Chad Stanley]] (one touchback in 70 punts) and [[Detroit Lions|Detroit]]'s [[Nick Harris (punter)|Nick Harris]] (two touchbacks in 84 punts). His ratio of touchbacks-to-punts is best for any 49ers punter since 1970, topping [[Joe Prokop]] (one touchback in 40 punts) in 1991.

====2006 season====
In 2006, Lee registered 81 punts (44.8 avg.) with 22 punts dropped inside the 20-yard line and a net average of 36.8. He finished seventh in NFL with 36.8 net yards, while his 44.8 gross average marked team’s highest since Tommy Davis averaged 45.6 in 1964. Lee was awarded game ball for his efforts in the 20–14 victory vs. Seattle (11–19) when he landed two punts inside the 20-yard line to help the 49ers win the battle of field position. He also grossed 51.5 yards per punt at St. Louis (11–26), which included a season-long of 66 yards.

====2007 season====
Lee earned Pro Bowl and All-Pro honors in 2007 after setting numerous records on 105 punts (47.3 avg.) with a net average of 41.0 and NFL record 42 punts downed inside opponents’ 20-yard line.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2007 NFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2007/probowl.htm |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |archive-date=March 16, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180316023313/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2007/probowl.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> His yardage, gross average, net average and punts downed inside 20-yard line all set team records. His 4,968 punting yards in 2007 are an NFL single season record. His 42 punts downed inside 20-yard line broke [[Baltimore Ravens|Baltimore's]] [[Kyle Richardson (punter)|Kyle Richardson's]] NFL mark of 39 in 1999. His 41.0 net average ranks second all-time in NFL history, trailing only [[Shane Lechler]] of Oakland (41.1 in 2007). He ranked second in NFL for gross average (47.3) and net punting average (41.0) to Oakland's Lechler. Also led the NFL with 49 punts over 50+ yards, which was 16 more than second ranked St. Louis’ [[Donnie Jones]] (33). Recorded four games in which he dropped four punts inside 20-yard line. Lee played key role in 49ers 37–31 overtime victory at Arizona (11–25), booming a 58-yard punt in overtime that wound up pinning Cardinals on their own three-yard line. The punt helped set up 49ers winning touchdown on DT [[Ronald Fields]] sack and forced fumble in the end zone that was recovered by linebacker [[Tully Banta-Cain]] for game-winning score.

====2008 season====
[[File:Joe Nedney kicks PAT at Rams at 49ers 11-16-08.JPG|thumb|[[San Francisco 49ers]] kicker [[Joe Nedney]] prepares to kick an extra point with punter Lee as the holder, 2008.]]
After earning Pro Bowl and All-Pro honors in 2007, Lee once again put up outstanding numbers, in 2008, as he set a career-high and team record with his 47.8 gross average. He had a career long 82-yard punt against the [[New England Patriots]] on October 5.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New England Patriots at San Francisco 49ers – October 5th, 2008 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200810050sfo.htm |access-date=December 16, 2017 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=December 17, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171217014742/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200810050sfo.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

====2009 season====
In the 2009 season, Lee returned to his 2007 form, having a superb year and earning his second Pro Bowl selection.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2009 NFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2009/probowl.htm |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=August 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180821031640/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2009/probowl.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

====2010 season====
Lee followed up his Pro Bowl season in 2009 with another stellar year for the 49ers, playing in all 16 games and averaging 46.2 yards per punt. The 2010 season also marked the first season a punter ran for more than 70 yards in a single game, as he completed 2 successful fake punt run attempts.

====2011 season====
In 2011, Lee set a new NFL single-season record by averaging 44.0 net yards per punt, while his gross average of 50.9 yards was third best in league history.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Price, Taylor |date=May 23, 2012 |title=Andy Lee Valued in San Francisco |url=http://www.49ers.com/news/article-2/Andy-Lee-Valued-in-San-Francisco/2c44d7fd-c12a-42cf-b96d-8faf1f81911a |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120628124337/http://www.49ers.com/news/article-2/Andy-Lee-Valued-in-San-Francisco/2c44d7fd-c12a-42cf-b96d-8faf1f81911a |archive-date=June 28, 2012 |access-date=June 17, 2012 |website=49ers.com}}</ref> He was named First-team All-Pro by the [[Associated Press]] and was voted to his third Pro Bowl.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2011 NFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2011/probowl.htm |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=August 30, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180830174119/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2011/probowl.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

====2012 season====
[[File:Andy Lee - San Francisco vs Green Bay 2012.jpg|thumb|Lee in 2012]]On May 25, 2012, Lee received a six-year $20.4 million contract extension with the 49ers that made him the third highest-paid punter in the league.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 25, 2012 |title=Breaking down Andy Lee's contract |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/breaking-down-andy-lee-s-contract-09000d5d82956692 |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=NFL.com |archive-date=December 2, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231202093440/https://www.nfl.com/news/breaking-down-andy-lee-s-contract-09000d5d82956692 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the 2012 regular season, Lee had 67	punts with a 48.15 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2012 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2012/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810232336/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2012/ |url-status=live }}</ref> At the end of the 2012 season, Lee and the 49ers appeared in [[Super Bowl XLVII]]. In the game, he had three punts for 159 net yards (55.0 average) as the 49ers fell to the [[Baltimore Ravens]] by a score of 34–31.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XLVII – San Francisco 49ers vs. Baltimore Ravens – February 3rd, 2013 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201302030sfo.htm |access-date=December 2, 2017 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=October 8, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211008105849/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201302030sfo.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>
====2013 season====
In the 2013 season, Lee had 79 punts with a 48.15 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2013 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2013/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810230712/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2013/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

====2014 season====
[[File:Andy Lee (American football).JPG|thumb|Lee in 2014|left]]In the 2014 season, Lee had 72 punts with a 46.79 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2014 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2014/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Cleveland Browns===
On June 6, 2015, Lee was traded to [[Cleveland Browns]] for a seventh-round pick in the [[2017 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sessler |first=Marc |date=June 6, 2015 |title=Browns acquire 49ers punter Andy Lee for draft pick |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/browns-acquire-49ers-punter-andy-lee-for-draft-pick-0ap3000000495925 |access-date=June 6, 2015 |website=NFL.com |archive-date=September 25, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200925065752/https://www.nfl.com/news/browns-acquire-49ers-punter-andy-lee-for-draft-pick-0ap3000000495925 |url-status=live }}</ref> This took place after the [[San Francisco 49ers|49ers]] drafted punter [[Bradley Pinion]]. He announced he would wear #8 for the team in honor of his daughter Madelyn, who died in February 2015 at just eight days old.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gribble |first=Andrew |date=June 11, 2015 |title=Browns punter Andy Lee to honor late daughter with new jersey number |url=http://www.clevelandbrowns.com/news/article-5/Browns-punter-Andy-Lee-to-honor-late-daughter-with-new-jersey-number/57ed2824-949e-4200-912a-5f4c025d9296 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150611204932/https://www.clevelandbrowns.com/news/article-5/Browns-punter-Andy-Lee-to-honor-late-daughter-with-new-jersey-number/57ed2824-949e-4200-912a-5f4c025d9296 |archive-date=June 11, 2015 |access-date=June 11, 2015 |website=ClevelandBrowns.com}}</ref> In the 2015 season, Lee had 70 punts with a 46.71 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2015 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2015/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Carolina Panthers===
On August 29, 2016, Lee was traded from the Browns to the [[Carolina Panthers]] along with a 2017 seventh-round pick for a 2018 fourth-round pick and punter [[Kasey Redfern]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Patra |first=Kevin |date=August 29, 2016 |title=Browns trade punter Andy Lee to Carolina Panthers |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/browns-trade-punter-andy-lee-to-carolina-panthers-0ap3000000692242 |access-date=August 29, 2016 |website=NFL.com |archive-date=August 14, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200814151653/https://www.nfl.com/news/browns-trade-punter-andy-lee-to-carolina-panthers-0ap3000000692242 |url-status=live }}</ref> Lee was placed on injured reserve on November 14, 2016, after pulling his hamstring.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Henson |first=Max |date=November 14, 2016 |title=Andy Lee placed on IR; Michael Palardy signed |url=http://www.panthers.com/news/article-2/Andy-Lee-placed-on-IR-Michael-Palardy-signed/6beda071-27df-4e6b-a32e-851a1e30df22 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161115193229/https://www.panthers.com/news/article-2/Andy-Lee-placed-on-IR-Michael-Palardy-signed/6beda071-27df-4e6b-a32e-851a1e30df22 |archive-date=November 15, 2016 |website=Panthers.com}}</ref>

On September 2, 2017, Lee was released by the Panthers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Henson |first=Max |date=September 2, 2017 |title=Panthers trim roster to 53 |url=http://www.panthers.com/news/article-2/Panthers-trim-roster-to-53/04544b8e-4a01-4568-9141-9ed61d2d4c51 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170920201032/https://www.panthers.com/news/article-2/Panthers-trim-roster-to-53/04544b8e-4a01-4568-9141-9ed61d2d4c51 |archive-date=September 20, 2017 |website=Panthers.com}}</ref>

===Arizona Cardinals===

==== 2017 season ====
On September 4, 2017, the [[Arizona Cardinals]] signed Lee to a two-year deal.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Urban |first=Darren |date=September 4, 2017 |title=Cardinals Sign Punter Andy Lee |url=http://www.azcardinals.com/news-and-events/article-2/Cardinals-Sign-Punter-Andy-Lee/b91509f5-638f-44ea-8e9f-2f8568dee3e9 |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=AZCardinals.com}}</ref> In the 2017 season, he had 88 punts with a 47.26 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2017 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2017/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

==== 2018 season ====
On June 14, 2018, Lee signed a two-year contract extension with the Cardinals through the 2020 season.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 14, 2018 |title=Andy Lee Signs Two-Year Extension |url=https://www.azcardinals.com/news/punter-andy-lee-signs-two-year-extension |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=AZCardinals.com |archive-date=March 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230328153731/https://www.azcardinals.com/news/punter-andy-lee-signs-two-year-extension |url-status=live }}</ref> In the 2018 season, he led with the league with 94 punts for 4,568 yards for a 48.6 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2018 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2018/ |access-date=November 22, 2019 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=October 29, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211029080055/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2018/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2018 NFL Leaders and Leaderboards |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2018/leaders.htm |access-date=November 22, 2019 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=December 31, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181231092604/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2018/leaders.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== 2019 season ====
During Week 10 against the [[2019 Tampa Bay Buccaneers|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], Lee converted on a 25-yard pass to [[Pharoh Cooper]] on a fake punt.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 10, 2019 |title=Winston rallies Bucs past Cardinals to snap skid |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/football-nfl-tb-ari-idUSMTZXEFBARWPBKD |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=Reuters |language=en |archive-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810232315/https://www.reuters.com/article/football-nfl-tb-ari-idUSMTZXEFBARWPBKD |url-status=live }}</ref> In the 2019 season, Lee had 61 punts with a 47.75 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2019 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2019/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

==== 2020 season ====
During Week 15 against the [[2020 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]], Lee converted on a 26-yard pass to [[linebacker]] [[Zeke Turner|Ezekiel Turner]] on a fake punt.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Raley |first=Dan |date=December 20, 2020 |title=Mr. Fourth Down: No One Does It Better than Ex-Husky Zeke Turner |url=https://www.si.com/college/washington/legends/no-one-does-fourth-down-better-than-ex-husky-zeke-turner |access-date=August 10, 2023 |magazine=Sports Illustrated |language=en |archive-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810232441/https://www.si.com/college/washington/legends/no-one-does-fourth-down-better-than-ex-husky-zeke-turner |url-status=live }}</ref> Lee finished the 2020 season with 58 punts for a 44.83 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2020 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2020/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en |archive-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810232640/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2020/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== 2021 season ====
Lee re-signed to a one-year contract with the Cardinals on March 22, 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Urban |first=Darren |date=March 22, 2021 |title=Some Work Done In Free Agency For Cardinals, Some Holes Left |url=https://www.azcardinals.com/news/some-work-done-in-free-agency-for-cardinals-some-holes-left |access-date=March 22, 2021 |website=AZCardinals.com |archive-date=March 22, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210322215629/https://www.azcardinals.com/news/some-work-done-in-free-agency-for-cardinals-some-holes-left |url-status=live }}</ref> In the 2021 season, he punted 51 times with a 49.04 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2021 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2021/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}}</ref>

==== 2022 season ====
Lee signed another one-year contract on March 17, 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Urban |first=Darren |date=March 17, 2022 |title=Cardinals Sign Long Snapper Aaron Brewer, Keep Andy Lee |url=https://www.azcardinals.com/news/cardinals-sign-long-snapper-aaron-brewer-keep-andy-lee |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=AZCardinals.com |archive-date=October 3, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231003035310/https://www.azcardinals.com/news/cardinals-sign-long-snapper-aaron-brewer-keep-andy-lee |url-status=live }}</ref> In the 2022 season, he punted 67 times with a 47.12 average.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Lee 2022 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2022/ |access-date=August 10, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |archive-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810232637/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/L/LeexAn20/gamelog/2022/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Becht''' (born August 8, 1977) is an American professional [[American football|football]] coach, broadcaster and former player who is the head coach of the [[Orlando Storm]] of the [[United Football League (2024–present)|United Football League]] (UFL) and color commentator for the [[New York Jets]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played as a [[tight end]] in the NFL for 11 seasons. Becht played [[college football]] for the [[West Virginia Mountaineers football|West Virginia Mountaineers]] and was selected by the Jets in the first round of the [[2000 NFL draft]] with the 27th overall pick. He was also a member of the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], [[St. Louis Rams]], [[Arizona Cardinals]], and [[Kansas City Chiefs]]. Becht was hired by [[ESPN College Football|ESPN]] as a college football analyst in 2013. He is also a co-host of the "Football Fan Shop" on the [[Home Shopping Network]]. In 2019, he was the [[tight ends coach]] of the [[San Diego Fleet]] of the [[Alliance of American Football]]. Anthony Becht worked as an analyst for some [[Sunday Night Football (radio)|Sunday Night Football]] games on [[Westwood One]] in 2021. He signed on as the Jets' color commentator for the [[2024 New York Jets season|2024 season]].{{Cite web |last=Florio |first=Mike |author-link=Mike Florio |date=2024-08-09 |title=Anthony Becht will spend UFL offseason working Jets games |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/anthony-becht-will-spend-ufl-offseason-working-jets-games |access-date=2024-08-11 |website=[[ProFootballTalk]] |language=en-US}} ==Personal life== Becht, a graduate of [[Monsignor Bonner High School]] in [[Drexel Hill, Pennsylvania]], was 6'5" and 205 pounds coming out of [[High school football|high school]]. Becht was an all-city, all-Catholic conference and all-county selection as a senior after recording 47 receptions for 693 yards. Becht accepted a football scholarship from [[West Virginia Mountaineers football|West Virginia]]. Becht’s son, [[Rocco Becht]], currently plays [[quarterback]] for [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State]] after playing three seasons for [[Iowa State Cyclones football|Iowa State]]. ==College career== At the end of Becht's college career, he ranked second among tight ends at the school with 83 catches for 1,173 yards, a 14.1 average of yards per catch, and 10 touchdowns. Becht was an honorable mention for [[All-American]] as a senior and was named second-team All-[[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East]] as a junior and senior, along with being team captain and [[Most valuable player|MVP]]. He graduated with a bachelor's degree in marketing. == Professional career== {{NFL predraft | height ft = 6 | height in = 5 5/8 | weight = 270 | dash = 4.69 | shuttle = 4.08 | cone drill = 6.94 | vertical = 33.5 | broad ft = 10 | broad in = 3 | arm span = 32 5/8 | hand span = 10 1/2 | note = All values from [[NFL Combine]]{{Cite web |title=2000 NFL Draft Scout Anthony Becht College Football Profile |url=https://draftscout.com/dsprofile.php?PlayerId=117&DraftYear=2000 |access-date=August 12, 2023 |website=DraftScout.com}}{{cite web | last=Battista | first=Judy | title=NFL Scouting Combine defined by league's need for speed | website=NFL.com | date=2014-02-14 | url=https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-scouting-combine-defined-by-league-s-need-for-speed-0ap2000000325783 | access-date=2025-05-11}} }} ===New York Jets=== Becht was selected by the Jets with a traded draft pick from Tampa Bay.{{Cite web |title=2000 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2000/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} As a [[rookie]] in [[2000 New York Jets season|2000]] for the Jets, Becht played in 14 games, missing two due to an ankle sprain. He was a [[Starting lineup|starter]] for 10 games and totaled 16 receptions for 144 yards and two touchdowns on the season. Becht ranked third among the rookie tight ends with receptions, behind [[Green Bay Packers|Green Bay's]] [[Bubba Franks]] and [[Cleveland Browns|Cleveland's]] [[Aaron Shea]]. In [[2001 New York Jets season|2001]], Becht started all 16 games and recorded 36 receptions for 321 yards and five touchdowns. He tied former [[New York Jets|Jets']] tight end [[Kyle Brady]] for the most receptions by an [[American Football Conference|AFC]] tight end. His five scores were only beat by [[Indianapolis Colts|Colts']] [[Marcus Pollard]] and [[Kansas City Chiefs|Chiefs']] [[Tony Gonzalez]]. Becht recorded consecutive game-winning touchdown catches in weeks 13 and 14. In [[2002 New York Jets season|2002]], Becht once again started all 16 games and tallied 28 receptions, 243 yards, and a career-high tying five scores. Becht caught one pass for eight yards and served as a key blocker in the 41–0 win over the Colts in the [[NFL playoffs, 2002-03#AFC: New York Jets 41.2C Indianapolis Colts 0|AFC Wild Card playoff game]] and recorded three receptions for 14 yards in the [[NFL playoffs, 2002-03#AFC: Oakland Raiders 30.2C New York Jets 10|AFC Divisional Playoff]] loss at [[Oakland Raiders|Oakland]]. In [[2003 New York Jets season|2003]], Becht set career-highs of 40 receptions for 356 yards and he included four TD catches while starting all sixteen games once again. Becht caught a career-best six passes, including a one-yard touchdown, and gained 32 yards at [[Miami Dolphins|Miami]] in the season finale. As his final season as a Jet in [[2004 New York Jets season|2004]], Becht had a career-low 13 receptions, for also lows of 100 yards and only 1 touchdown. He did manage to catch a touchdown pass in the Jets Wild Card win over the [[San Diego Chargers]]. In [[New York City]], Becht totaled 1,146 yards receiving with 17 touchdowns off of 133 receptions. ===Tampa Bay Buccaneers=== In his first year in [[Tampa Bay, Florida|Tampa Bay]] in [[2005 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|2005]], Becht recorded 16 receptions, much like his rookie year, 112 yards but no touchdowns as his career began to slide downward. Becht competed with rookie [[Alex Smith (tight end)|Alex Smith]] for the tight end spot, who the Bucs picked up in the [[2005 NFL draft]]. In [[2006 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|2006]], Becht saw himself being replaced by the rookie, Smith. Still, Becht grabbed 18 receptions for 115 yards and a score, from mainly rookie [[Bruce Gradkowski]]. In 2007, Becht's productivity decreased even more. He finished the season with only 5 receptions for 201 yards and 2 touchdowns. ===St. Louis Rams=== On March 6, 2008, he signed with the [[St. Louis Rams]]. Becht joined fellow-former [[West Virginia Mountaineers|Mountaineers]] [[Marc Magro]] and [[Marc Bulger]] on the Rams squad. Becht played one season with the team before his release on March 12, 2009. [[File:JetsVsRams 2008 (cropped)2.jpg|thumb|Becht with the [[St. Louis Rams]] in 2008]] ===Arizona Cardinals=== Becht signed with the [[Arizona Cardinals]] on March 19, 2009. In [[2009 Arizona Cardinals season|2009]], Becht had 61 yards on 10 catches, averaging 6.1 yards per catch. He also had one receiving touchdown. On September 3, 2010, Becht was released as part of final cuts for the [[2010 NFL season]]. ===Kansas City Chiefs=== Becht signed with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] on August 25, 2011, but was released on September 5. The Chiefs re-signed him on September 16. Becht was released by the Chiefs again, so there could be room for tight end [[Jake O'Connell]]. On October 26, he was signed once again, by the Chiefs. '''Andrew Jon McCollum''' (born June 2, 1970) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (American football)|center]] for 15 seasons in the [[National Football League]] for three teams. He played [[college football]] at [[Toledo Rockets football|Toledo Rockets]]. He was signed by the [[Milwaukee Mustangs (1994–2001)|Milwaukee Mustangs]] as a [[street free agent]] in 1994.

McCollum also played for the [[New Orleans Saints]], [[St. Louis Rams]], and [[Detroit Lions]]. He earned a [[Super Bowl ring]] with the Rams in [[Super Bowl XXXIV]].

==Early life==
McCollum attended [[Revere High School (Ohio)|Revere High School]] in [[Richfield, Ohio]].

==New Orleans Saints==
McCollum was a center and guard for the New Orleans Saints from 1994 to 1999.<ref name=pfr>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/McCoAn20.htm|title=Andy McCollum Stats|publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com|accessdate=February 2, 2024}}</ref>

==St. Louis Rams==
In his first year with the Rams (1999), McCollum was a reserve offensive lineman of the winning team of [[Super Bowl XXXIV]]. McCollum took over from [[Mike Gruttadauria]] as the starting center for the St. Louis Rams in his second year with that team (2000), the first under first-time NFL head coach [[Mike Martz]], their offensive coordinator of the previous year.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/st-louis-post-dispatch-feature-piece-on/140129055/|title=McCollum has quiet image, but his persistence speaks volumes|first=Nick|last=Wishart|work=[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]]|date=November 25, 2001|page=56|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{open access}}</ref> Thanks to a strong offensive line of McCollum, guards [[Tom Nütten]] and [[Adam Timmerman]], and tackles [[Orlando Pace]] and [[Ryan Tucker]], the Rams won a wildcard playoff berth with a 10–6 won-lost record and 540 points scored (33.8 points per game, 1st in the NFL), but lost a wild card game of the [[2000–01 NFL playoffs]] to the New Orleans Saints, despite [[Kurt Warner]]'s 365 yards in the air, the offensive line allowing 2 sacks for 15 yards. The following year, the Rams' record was a powerful 14–2 and 503 points scored (31.4 points per game, 1st in the NFL), winning the west division title again. In the [[2001–02 NFL playoffs]] with the same offensive line except for [[Rod Jones (offensive lineman)]] replacing Tucker at right tackle, St. Louis won the divisional round game against the [[Green Bay Packers]] and the NFC championship game against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] with over 200 net passing yards in each game. However, the Rams lost [[Super Bowl XXXVI]] to the [[New England Patriots]], despite 337 net passing yards. In 2002, Warner was injured for most of the year, replaced by [[Marc Bulger]], less effective as the Rams missed the playoffs with a record of 7–9.

With Bulger as the new quarterback, and Warner in reserve, St. Louis came back strong in 2003 with a 12–4 record, 1st in the [[NFC West]], and 447 points scored (27.9 points/game), 2nd in the NFL. However, in the [[2003–04 NFL playoffs]], the Rams lost to the [[Carolina Panthers]] in the divisional round, despite 316 net passing yards. In that game, as well as throughout the year, McCollum played left guard in place of the injured Nütten, with [[Dave Wohlabaugh]] at center. In 2004, with Bulger as the regular starter and McCollum back at center, the team was only 8–8, but still qualified for a wild card game in the [[2004–05 NFL playoffs]], beating the [[Seattle Seahawks]] with the same basic offensive line (McCollum at center, Nütten and Timmerman at guards, Pace and a new offensive right tackle, [[Blaine Saipaia]]. However, the Rams lost 47–17 in the divisional round to the [[Atlanta Falcons]], as they could not control [[Michael Vick]]'s running and passing. The Rams did not make the playoffs in McCollum's last three years with the team, up to 2007, when their record was a dismal 3–13.

McCollum started all 16 games for six years from 2000 to 2005, but played and started in one game in 2006 and started in 10 games in 2007. In 2006, he was replaced as the starting center by [[Richie Incognito]]. However, Incognito was injured through most of 2007, starting in four games, so McCollum returned briefly as the starter. In 2008, Incognito became the starting right guard, and [[Brett Romberg]], among others, became the center.

==Detroit Lions==
McCollum ended his career in 2008, starting in four games, playing in 12, for a [[Detroit Lions]] team that finished with a 0–16 record.<ref name=pfr/>

'''Anthony Abayomi Alabi''' ({{IPAc-en|ə|ˈ|l|ɑː|b|i}}; born February 16, 1981) is an American [[actor]] and former professional [[American football|football]] [[offensive tackle]]. He was selected by the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the fifth round of the [[2005 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] at [[TCU Horned Frogs football|TCU]].

Alabi was also a member of the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]].

Since 2010, Alabi has been acting. His most recent role is in the [[Netflix]] series [[Family Reunion (TV series)|''Family Reunion''.]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.romper.com/p/who-plays-moz-on-family-reunion-anthony-alabi-is-no-stranger-to-the-spotlight-18185166|title=Anthony Alabi Is Bringing His A-Game To Netflix's New Sitcom 'Family Reunion'|website=Romper|date=10 July 2019 |language=en|access-date=2019-07-13}}</ref>

==Early life==
Alabi attended [[Antonian College Preparatory High School]] in San Antonio, where he was a four-year [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]], and also lettered in [[basketball]] and [[track and field]] ([[shot put]] and [[discus]]). He earned all-district and all-state honors in football and led the team in [[Quarterback sack|sacks]] (13) and [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]] (82) as a senior.  He was a two-time state champion in track. Alabi was inducted in the 2013–14 Antonian Athletics Hall of Fame class.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.antonian.org/apps/pages/index.jsp?uREC_ID=237028&type=d&pREC_ID=546348 |title=Anthony Alabi (ACP '99) – Athletic Hall of Fame Inductees – Antonian College Preparatory High School |accessdate=April 7, 2021 |publisher=antonian.org }}{{Dead link|date=October 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

==College career==
Alabi attended the [[United States Naval Academy]] for a short time in 1999 before heading to [[Texas Christian University| Texas Christian University (TCU)]], where he was a four-year letterman, [[Starting lineup|starting]] his final three seasons and making 35 career starts in college. He was a [[defensive lineman]] before moving to the [[offensive line]] during his [[Redshirt (college sports)|redshirt]] season in 2000. He started all 12 games at left tackle as a sophomore, as TCU led the [[Conference USA]] by averaging 203.2 yards rushing per outing. As a junior, he was part of a line that paved the way for an offense that averaged more than 200 net rushing yards and 200 net passing yards per game – one of only six [[Division I (NCAA)|Division I]] schools to accomplish that feat. In his senior season, the offense averaged 32.9 points per game. He earned first-team All-Conference USA accolades each of his final two years, during which time he opened a combined 23 games.

===Miami Dolphins===
Alabi was selected by the Miami Dolphins in the fifth round (162nd overall) of the 2005 NFL draft by former [[head coach]] [[Nick Saban]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The pick used to select him was acquired from the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the deal that sent [[cornerback]] [[Patrick Surtain]] to the Chiefs. On July 22, the Dolphins signed Alabi to a four-year contract that included a signing bonus of $158,000.

Alabi was tried at left tackle during [[National Football League Training Camp|training camp]], and shortly after returning to practice from an ankle injury he was shifted to right tackle. He played in a reserve role during the team's five preseason games, and was inactive for all 16 regular season contests. He nursed an elbow injury during November which caused him to miss practice time.

Alabi saw his first regular season action in [[2006 Miami Dolphins season|2006]], playing in six games during the year. He made his NFL debut in a reserve role on October 1 at the [[Houston Texans]]. He also saw extensive action on December 17 at the [[Buffalo Bills]] following injury to [[Damion McIntosh]].

On February 11, Alabi was one of nine players let go by the Dolphins.

===Kansas City Chiefs===
On February 13, just two days after being waived by the Dolphins, Alabi was claimed by the Kansas City Chiefs. Alabi was released by the Chiefs on August 30, 2008.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/2008/08/30/chiefs_place_merritt_on_nfi_release_21_others/ |title=Chiefs Place Merritt on NFI; Release 21 Others |accessdate=2008-09-16 |publisher=kcchiefs.com |date=August 30, 2008 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080905185800/http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/2008/08/30/chiefs_place_merritt_on_nfi_release_21_others/ |archivedate=5 September 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Tampa Bay Buccaneers===
After spending the 2008 regular season out of football, Alabi was signed to a reserve/future contract by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on January 6, 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.buccaneers.com/news/early-signing-period-2187273 |title=Early Signing Period |accessdate=April 7, 2021 |publisher=buccaneers.com |date=January 7, 2009}}</ref><ref name="nbcsportsedge.com"/>

Alabi was released by the Buccaneers on September 5, 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.spotrac.com/nfl/tampa-bay-buccaneers/anthony-alabi-6021/transactions/ |title=Anthony Alabi Contract Breakdowns, Salary Cap Figures, Salaries, Bonuses |accessdate=April 7, 2021 |publisher=spotrac.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://sportsforecaster.com/nfl/player/6777/trans |title=Anthony Alabi Stats, Profile, Bio, Analysis and More |accessdate=April 7, 2021 |publisher=sportsforecaster.com }}{{Dead link|date=October 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

==Acting career==
Alabi retired from the NFL in 2009 to pursue a career in acting. He is a series lead in ''[[Family Reunion (TV series)|Family Reunion]]'', a [[Netflix]] original series also starring [[Loretta Devine]], [[Tia Mowry]], and [[Richard Roundtree]], which released in July 2019. He also has recurring roles in ''[[Raven's Home]]'' and ''[[Bosch (TV series)|Bosch]]'' as well as guest star roles in ''[[Malibu Rescue]]'', ''[[Shameless (American TV series)|Shameless]]'', and ''[[Insecure (TV series)|Insecure]]''. He also played Guldan in the [[Hearthstone]] "Mulligans" web series by [[Blizzard Entertainment]].

'''Anthony Devon Cannon''' (born December 31, 1984) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Detroit Lions]] in the seventh round of the [[2006 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2006 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2006/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-10 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Tulane Green Wave football|Tulane Green Wave]]. He was also a member of the [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL).

==Professional career==

===Detroit Lions===
The Lions drafted Cannon in the seventh round in 2006. He played in 32 games for Detroit over three seasons and made 21 tackles. Cannon was released by the Lions on March 16, 2009, after three seasons with the team.<ref>{{cite web |title=Anthony Cannon Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/C/CannAn20.htm |website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |access-date=27 June 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

===Toronto Argonauts===
On January 6, 2011, Cannon signed with the [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the [[Canadian Football League]]. In the [[2011 CFL season]] Cannon accumulated 51 tackles. Cannon was released by the Argonauts prior to the start of the [[2012 CFL season]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cfl.ca/article/smalls-cannon-headline-argos-cuts |title=Smalls, Cannon headline Argos cuts | CFL.ca | Official Site of the Canadian Football League |accessdate=2012-06-21 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622095631/http://www.cfl.ca/article/smalls-cannon-headline-argos-cuts |archivedate=2012-06-22 }} Argonauts release Cannon.</ref>

'''Charles Andrew Russell''' (October 29, 1941 – March 1, 2024) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who spent his entire 12-year career as a [[linebacker]] for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

==Early life ==
Russell was born October 29, 1941, in [[Detroit|Detroit, Michigan]] to a family that relocated multiple times in his childhood (to Chicago and New York) due to his father's work as an executive with the [[Monsanto]] chemical company. The family eventually settled in Ladue, a suburb of [[St. Louis]], when Russell was a 7th grader. He grew up wanting to be a businessman.<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Bouchette |first=Ed |date=June 14, 1981 |title=Andy Russell |work=Sunday-The Daily News (Lebanon, Pennsylvania) |pages=50}}</ref><ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Broeg |first=Bob |date=January 8, 1975 |title=Steelers' Russell A 'Super' Blue Chipper |work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |pages=52}}</ref>

He attended [[Ladue Horton Watkins High School|Ladue High School]] where he played high school football and basketball. He was nicknamed "the Horse" for his power, and was known for his use of the [[Stiff-arm fend|stiff-arm]] as a runner. In a 1958 football game played on [[Halloween]], Russell scored five touchdowns as a [[Fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]]. He scored 121 points total in 1958, and that team was undefeated and won its league's title. He was also on the [[Track and field|track]] team, and had once set a [[low hurdles]] record. Russell graduated in 1959.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Posen |first=Bob |date=November 1, 1958 |title=5 Russell TDs Spark Ladue Win |work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |pages=7}}</ref><ref name=":7">[https://alumni.ladueschools.net/distinguished-alumni-2002/ "Distinguished Alumni"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181011053513/https://alumni.ladueschools.net/distinguished-alumni-2002/ |date=2018-10-11 }}. Ladue Education Foundation and Alumni Association. Accessed February 8, 2018.</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Andy Russell Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RussAn00.htm |access-date=2025-01-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite news |date=April 26, 1959 |title=Grid Scholarship At Missouri for Ladue's Russell |work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |pages=79}}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite news |last=Kee |first=Howard |date=December 7, 1958 |title=Russell Tops Voting For All-District |work=St. Louis Globe-Democrat |pages=85}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=April 27, 1958 |title=Ladue's Record Spree Takes Little Six Senior |work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |pages=66}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Archibald |first=John J. |date=November 13, 1958 |title=Ladue and Burroughs Coaches Post Credits for Perfect Seasons |work=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |pages=63}}</ref>  

In football, as a senior Russell was named an All-American by ''[[The Sporting News]]'' and was first team all-state.<ref name=":8" /> He received the most votes of the all-district team selected by the ''[[St. Louis Globe-Democrat]]''.<ref name=":9" />

== College ==
Heavily recruited by out-state universities, he selected the [[University of Missouri]] which gave him an athletic scholarship. Under Coach [[Dan Devine]] he played both linebacker and fullback. In his three seasons (1960–1962) with the team, they lost just four times (with [[1960 Missouri Tigers football team|one loss later vacated]]) while Russell led the team in rushing (1961) and interceptions (1962). In addition to his football talents, he graduated with a bachelor's degree in [[economics]] in 1963.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://pittsburghquarterly.com/articles/andy-russell-businessman-and-former-steeler/ | title=Andy Russell, Businessman and Former Steeler }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Russell College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/andy-russell-1.html |access-date=2025-01-31 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1961 Missouri Tigers Stats |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/missouri/1961.html |access-date=2025-01-31 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":8" /> He played in the [[Bluebonnet Bowl|Blue Bonnet Bowl]] for Missouri.<ref name=":3" /> He never missed a game in high school or college.<ref name=":4" />

==Playing career==
His father did not wish for him to play professional football, and Russell put a "no" on every questionnaire mailed to him by prospective NFL teams. However, the one team that did not send him a letter was the one who drafted him in the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://retrosimba.com/2024/03/29/cardinals-fumbled-chance-to-land-local-lad-andy-russell/ | title=Cardinals fumbled chance to land local lad Andy Russell | date=March 29, 2024 }}</ref> However, he elected to sign for a $12,000 salary and a $3,000 signing bonus. After playing for the Steelers his rookie season in [[1963 Pittsburgh Steelers season|1963]], Russell temporarily left the team for the [[United States Army|Army]] to fulfill [[Reserve Officers' Training Corps|ROTC]] commitments that had him stationed in Germany.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/playoffs2008/news/story?page=hotread19/chucknoll|title=Merrill: The lessons of Chuck Noll|date=21 January 2009}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> He then returned to the Steelers in 1966, having convinced his father that it would be best for him to play football to pay for further studies in economics for a master's degree. Russell would play the next eleven seasons and graduate with an [[Master of Business Administration|M.B.A.]] from Missouri in economics/finance in 1967 (the following year, he formed his own company involving investment vehicle syndicates).<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Sewald |first=Jeff |date=February 20, 2006 |title=Andy Russell, Businessman and Former Steeler |url=https://pittsburghquarterly.com/articles/andy-russell/ |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=Pittsburgh Quarterly |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Labriola |first=Bob |date=March 2, 2024 |title=1970s team captain Andy Russell, 82 |url=https://www.steelers.com/news/1970s-team-captain-andy-russell-82 |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=www.steelers.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

Russell was one of the few players future [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] and member of the [[NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team|NFL 100th Anniversary Team]] coach [[Chuck Noll]] kept, when he became the Steelers head coach in 1969. Russell was an early member of Pittsburgh's famed [[Steel Curtain]] defense and was named the Steelers' [[Most valuable player|MVP]] in 1971. He made seven [[Pro Bowl]] appearances—in 1969 and from 1971 through 1976—and earned two [[Super Bowl ring]]s in [[Super Bowl IX]] and [[Super Bowl X]].<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":1" /> When future Pro Football Hall of Fame linebacker [[Jack Ham]] joined the team as a rookie in 1971, Russell took the time to mentor Ham, contrary to the usual customs of veteran-rookie interactions at the time.<ref name=":5" /> 

On December 27, 1975, Russell set the NFL playoff record for a returned touchdown–93 yards in a [[Three Rivers Stadium]] victory over the [[Baltimore Colts]]. Some have claimed it as the longest football play from scrimmage in time duration.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Steelers tell jokes, share tales at 75th year gala |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/sports/steelers/2007/11/05/Steelers-tell-jokes-share-tales-at-75th-year-gala/stories/200711050227 |access-date=2022-10-20 |website=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |language=en}}</ref> The record was broken with a 98 yard return in 2023.<ref name=":0" />

He never missed a game, playing in 168 consecutive games for the Steelers.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Andy Russell {{!}} Pittsburgh Steelers - Steelers.com |url=https://www.steelers.com/history/bios/russell_andy |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=www.steelers.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2024-03-02 |title=Ex-Steelers LB Russell, 7-time Pro Bowler, dies |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/39638847/steelers-great-andy-russell-2-super-bowl-champ-dies-82 |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref> His teammates voted him team captain for ten seasons.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":1" /> He was named a member of the Steelers All-Time Team and the NFL’s All-Decade Team for the 1970s.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Remembering the life of ANDY RUSSELL |url=https://obituaries.post-gazette.com/obituary/andy-russell-1089436150 |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=obituaries.post-gazette.com |language=en}}</ref> In 2017, he was an inaugural member into the Steelers Hall of Honor.<ref name=":2" /> Russell was one of only four inductees, out of a class of twenty-seven, who were not in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Klinger |first=Jacob |date=2017-11-27 |title=Steelers remember 27 in inaugural Hall of Honor induction ceremony |url=https://www.pennlive.com/steelers/2017/11/steelers_hall_of_honor.html |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=pennlive |language=en}}</ref>

In 1976, he was inducted into the [[Missouri Sports Hall of Fame]] and to the Mizzou Athletics Hall of Fame in 1993. In 2011, the [[Professional Football Researchers Association]] named Russell to the PFRA Hall of Very Good Class of 2011.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.profootballresearchers.com/hall-of-very-good-2011.htm |title=Hall of Very Good Class of 2011 |access-date=November 23, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180902011938/http://www.profootballresearchers.com/hall-of-very-good-2011.htm |archive-date=September 2, 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kerkhoff |first=Blair |date=2 March 2024 |title=Former Missouri Tigers & Pittsburgh Steelers great Andy Russell dies at 82 |url=https://www.kansascity.com/sports/college/sec/university-of-missouri/article286169011.html |access-date=28 September 2024 |website=kansascity.com}}</ref>

==Personal life==
After his playing days ended, Russell maintained his interest in business and investing to go along with endurance canoeing, mountain climbing, and philanthropy.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite news |date=August 13, 1977 |title=The Wilderness and Andy Russell |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/08/13/archives/the-wilderness-and-andy-russell.html |work=New York Times}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Russell's financial success came outside football, and he was an active entrepreneur involved in the investment business during and after his football career. He was a partner with various investment banking firms.<ref name=":2" /> 

Among his charitable and community service efforts, he founded the Andy Russell Charitable Foundation in 1999,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andy Russell Charitable Foundation {{!}} |url=https://andyrussell.org/ |access-date=2024-10-30 |language=en-US}}</ref> and generated over $10 million in contributions to [[UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh|Children's Hospital]] in Pittsburgh through the Andy Russell Charitable Golf Tournament. The foundation also supported charities and charitable causes such as [[Ronald McDonald House Charities|The Ronald McDonald House]], [[Blood Cancer United|Leukemia Society]], The Cancer Society, Economics PA, Cystic Fibrosis, Mothers Hope, Juvenile Diabetes, SIDS, and Pittsburgh Vision Services. Russell's most recent charitable work before his death was Everyone's Playground,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Everyone's Playground {{!}} Andy Russell Charitable Foundation |url=https://andyrussell.org/everyonesplayground/ |access-date=2024-10-30 |language=en-US}}</ref> a park for special needs children located in [[Selinsgrove, Pennsylvania]].<ref name=":2" /> 

In 1989, he was named Big Brothers and Sisters Man of the Year.<ref name=":5" /> 

Russell wrote three books, ''A Steeler Odyssey'' (1998), ''An Odd Steelers Journey'' (2002), and ''Beyond the Goalpost'' (2010).<ref name=":5" /> 

== Death ==
Russell died on March 1, 2024, at the age of 82.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Thompson |first1=Stephen |title=Steelers Great Andy Russell Passes at 82 |url=https://www.si.com/nfl/steelers/news/pittsburgh-steelers-great-andy-russell-passes-82#google_vignette |access-date=1 March 2024 |publisher=Si |date=1 March 2024}}</ref> He died of complications from [[Alzheimer's disease|Alzheimer’s Disease]] and [[respiratory syncytial virus]] (RSV).<ref name=":2" /> A memorial service for Russell was held on June 15, 2024, at Everyone's Playground.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Carlip |first=Freddi |date=2024-07-07 |title=Stellar Steelers star remembered at memorial service |url=https://www.dailyitem.com/stellar-steelers-star-remembered-at-memorial-service/article_56007b0c-380d-11ef-a3e4-7356ea55f8ef.html |access-date=2024-10-30 |website=The Daily Item |language=en}}</ref>

'''Andrew “Bro” Robert Thorn''' (born February 4, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] and [[Dallas Cowboys]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Northern Iowa Panthers football|Northern Iowa Panthers]].

==Early life==
Thorn attended [[Waterford Mott High School]], where he was a two-way player at [[tight end]] and [[defensive end]]. As a sophomore, he made 2 receptions for 15 yards. As a junior, he had 19 receptions for 270 yards, 3 [[touchdown]]s and received All-conference honors.<ref name="school">{{cite web | url=https://unipanthers.com/news/2004/7/29/205189321.aspx?path=football | title=UNI Signs 24 Football Players | accessdate=February 19, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181209125210/https://unipanthers.com/news/2004/7/29/205189321.aspx?path=football | archive-date=December 9, 2018 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

As a senior, he collected 25 receptions for 450 yards, 6 touchdowns, 68 tackles and 3 sacks. He set a school record with 3 [[touchdown]] receptions in a single-game. He helped his team finish with a 6–4 record and qualify to the state playoffs for the first time in school history, while receiving second-team All-Metro and All-county honors.<ref name=school/>

He also practiced [[basketball]], [[track & field|track]] and [[baseball]]. He set the school record in the [[shot put]] (57'9") and [[discus throw]] (172'9"). He received Academic All-state honors in his last 2 years.<ref name=school/>

==College career==
Thorn accepted a football scholarship from the [[University of Iowa]]. As a [[Redshirt (college sports)|redshirt]] freshman, he appeared in 4 games. As a sophomore, he saw limited action. He transferred to the Division I-AA [[University of Northern Iowa]] after the season.<ref name=school/>

As junior, he posted 17 receptions for 190 yards and 4 touchdowns.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://unipanthers.com/news/2004/9/3/205190580.aspx?path=football | title=UNI Opens Season At 1-A Iowa State Saturday | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref> As a senior, he registered 21 receptions for 308 yards and 6 touchdowns. He finished his college career with 38 receptions for 498 yards and 10 [[touchdown]]s.

==Professional career==
===Philadelphia Eagles===
Thorn was signed as an [[undrafted free agent]] by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] after the [[2005 NFL draft]] on April 25.<ref name="Transactions">{{cite web| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/09/04/sports/transactions.html | title=Transactions | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref> On September 3, he was waived and later signed to the [[practice squad]], where he spent the rest of the season.<ref name="Transactions"/> He was released on September 2, [[2006 NFL season|2006]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.courant.com/news/connecticut/hc-xpm-2006-09-03-0609030016-story.html | title=NFL Transactions | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.espn.com/espn/wire/_/section/nfl/id/2570830 | title=Eagles trade Fraley, Parry; cut Gaffney, Reed | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

===Dallas Cowboys===
On October 4, [[2006 NFL season|2006]], he was signed by the [[Dallas Cowboy]] to the [[practice squad]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.courant.com/news/connecticut/hc-xpm-2006-10-05-0610050175-story.html | title=NFL Transactions | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref> On December 14, he was promoted to the active roster to improve depth at [[tight end]] and [[H-back]], after [[Oliver Hoyte]] suffered a knee injury. He was cut after missing a curfew on August 9, [[2007 NFL season|2007]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.espn.com/dallas/nfl/columns/story?columnist=archer_todd&id=6806084 | title=Jason Garrett makes strong statement | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

===Tennessee Titans===
On August 22, [[2007 NFL season|2007]], he was signed as a [[free agent]] by the [[Tennessee Titans]], but was released 4 days later.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/trainingcamp07/news/story?id=2992182 | title=Former Pro Bowler Drummond signs with Kansas City | accessdate=February 19, 2018}}</ref>

'''Andrew Lee Maurer''' (September 30, 1948 – January 3, 2016) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[offensive lineman]] in the [[National Football League|NFL]] for the [[Atlanta Falcons]], [[New Orleans Saints]], [[Minnesota Vikings]], [[San Francisco 49ers]], and the [[Denver Broncos]].  He played in [[Super Bowl IX]] as a member of the Vikings and [[Super Bowl XII]] as a member of the Broncos.  He appeared in 109 regular season games, starting 84 of them.  Additionally, he started all seven playoff games he appeared in.  Maurer played [[college football]] at the [[University of Oregon]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/M/MaurAn20.htm|title=Andy Maurer|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref>

Maurer served as head football coach at Cascade Christian High School in Medford, Oregon, from 1992 to 2010.  He died of cancer on January 3, 2016, at the age of 67.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mailtribune.com/article/20160105/SPORTS/160109874|title=Ex-grid star, Challengers coach Maurer dies|author=Kris Henry|work=MailTribune.com}}</ref>

'''Anthony Derrick Allen''' (born June 29, 1959) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for five seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Atlanta Falcons]], [[Washington Redskins]], and [[San Diego Chargers]].  He played [[college football]] for the [[Washington Huskies football|Washington Huskies]] and was selected in the sixth round of the [[1983 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/draft/history/fulldraft?season=1983#round6 |title=NFL Draft History |work=nfl.com |access-date=January 4, 2013}}</ref>

==Professional playing career==
Allen made his professional debut in the [[United States Football League]] (USFL) in 1983.  Allen was originally drafted by the USFL's [[Tampa Bay Bandits]] in the third round of the [[1983 USFL draft]].  After being selected in the sixth round of the [[1983 NFL draft]], the [[Los Angeles Express (USFL)|Los Angeles Express]] acquired his USFL rights from the Bandits for a fourth-round pick the [[1984 USFL draft]].  He signed with the Express immediately and started the last eight games of the 1983 USFL season catching 37 passes for 613 yards and three touchdowns.

In 1984, Allen started the season with the Express, however, was traded mid-season to the [[Michigan Panthers]] for a draft pick after eight games.  The Panthers primarily acquired Allen to fill the void left when Panthers' star receiver [[Anthony Carter (American football)|Anthony Carter]] was lost for the season with a broken arm.  Allen finished the season with 34 receptions for 535 yards and touchdowns.

When the Panthers merged with the [[Oakland Invaders]] prior to the 1985 USFL season, Allen was not protected in the merger and was selected in the dispersal draft by the [[Philadelphia/Baltimore Stars|Baltimore Stars]].  He was released by the Stars and signed on with the [[Portland Breakers]] on April 3, 1985.  He played six games (starting three) for the Breakers catching nine passes for 133 yards and two touchdowns before being released on May 14.

In his first game as a wide receiver for the Redskins against the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]], Allen had eight catches for 255 yards and three touchdowns, which is still a franchise record.  It was the first game played during the [[National Football League Players Association#1987 strike and decertification|1987 NFL players' strike]].  While with the Redskins, Allen won a [[Super Bowl]].

==Coaching career==
From 2004 to 2010, Allen coached football at [[Garfield High School (Seattle, Washington)|Garfield High School]] in [[Seattle]], Washington.<ref name=MaxPreps>{{cite web|title=Garfield Coach History|url=http://www.maxpreps.com/local/team/records/coaches.aspx?gendersport=boys,football&schoolid=25d76539-4cdb-4da2-99ae-595d916a0181|work=CBS Sports}}</ref>

'''Anthony Eugene Anderson''' (born September 27, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Temple Owls football|Temple Owls]]. He played for two seasons in the NFL for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], where he won a [[Super Bowl ring]] in [[Super Bowl XIV]] against the [[Los Angeles Rams]], and also played with the [[Atlanta Falcons]]. Anderson played for the [[Philadelphia/Baltimore Stars|Philadelphia Stars]] of the [[United States Football League]] (USFL) in the 1983 season.<ref>{{cite web|title=Anthony Anderson|url=http://www.justsportsstats.com/footballstatsindex.php?player_id=anderant001|publisher=Stats Crew}}</ref><ref name=owl>{{cite web|title=Anthony Anderson|url=http://owlsports.com/hof.aspx?hof=236&path=&kiosk=|publisher=Owl Sports}}</ref>

==Playing career==
Anderson attended [[Thomas McKean High School]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anthony Anderson Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/A/AndeAn20.htm |access-date=2023-02-24 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> where he was a two-time All-Stater. In 1994, Anderson was inducted into the [[Delaware Sports Museum and Hall of Fame|Delaware Sports Hall of Fame]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Past Inductees |url=http://www.desports.org/past_inductees.html |publisher=Delaware Sports Museum and Hall of Fame |quote=1994 Anthony Anderson |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928214547/http://www.desports.org/past_inductees.html |archivedate=2011-09-28 }}</ref> and was also inducted into Temple University Hall of Fame.<ref name=owl/> Anderson was at the time the second leading ground-gainer in Temple football history. Anderson earned the All-East and All-American awards while at Temple.<ref name=owl/>

As part of the nationwide kickoff to the [[Super Bowl 50]] celebration, the NFL launched today the Super Bowl High School Honor Roll initiative recognizing schools and communities that contributed to Super Bowl history and positively impacted the game of football.<ref>{{Cite web|title = League launches Super Bowl High School Honor Roll|url = https://www.nfl.com/news/league-launches-super-bowl-high-school-honor-roll-0ap3000000524521|website = NFL.com|access-date = 2016-02-03}}</ref> On January 11, 2016, Anderson received this honor at Thomas McKean High School. That night, the high school also retired his jersey number.

==Personal life==
Anderson owns a construction company in Delaware and does motivational speaking engagements. Anderson had a small role in the made-for-TV movie, ''Fighting Back'', a story about [[Rocky Bleier]]. Anthony Anderson has a son named Anthony Brown who was a running back that played football for [[Wesley College (Delaware)|Wesley College]] in [[Dover, Delaware]]

His first start was in Week 11 on November 22, 2009 against the Pittsburgh Steelers, in place of injured [[Mike Vrabel]]. In his first start, he intercepted [[Ben Roethlisberger]] twice, as the Chiefs won the game.  On October 31, 2011 against the [[San Diego Chargers]], Studebaker recovered an unlikely fumbled snap by [[quarterback]] [[Philip Rivers]] from amongst the scrum, likely aiding the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in their improbable win that day by preventing the Chargers from scoring with just over a minute left in regulation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thorman |first=Joel |date=November 1, 2011 |title=How Did Andy Studebaker Come Away With The Philip Rivers Fumble? |url=https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2011/11/1/2530275/chiefs-andy-studebaker-philip-rivers-fumble |access-date=March 18, 2021 |website=Arrowhead Pride |language=en}}</ref> Studebaker had 16 tackles, one fumble recovery, and one forced fumble at the end of the season.<ref name="stats">{{Cite web |title=Andy Studebaker Stats - Pro-Football-Reference.com |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/StudAn99.htm |access-date=April 27, 2018 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref> While with the Chiefs, he was popularly known among fans as "The Student Baker."<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 23, 2010 |title=Hedging Our Bets |url=https://arrowheadaddict.com/2010/08/23/hedging-our-bets/ |access-date=March 18, 2021 |website=Arrowhead Addict |language=en-US}}</ref>

On April 1, 2013, the Chiefs released Studebaker.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Allen |first=Patrick |date=April 1, 2013 |title=Chiefs Release Andy Studebaker |url=https://arrowheadaddict.com/2013/04/01/chiefs-release-andy-studebaker/ |access-date=March 18, 2021 |website=Arrowhead Addict |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Jacksonville Jaguars===
Studebaker was signed by the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] on August 13, 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jaguars add LB Andy Studebaker |url=http://www.jaguars.com/news/article-PressRelease/Jaguars-add-LB-Andy-Studebaker/0de914a3-1ea5-4ba0-abd2-4fb48425d890 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180428011652/http://www.jaguars.com/news/article-PressRelease/Jaguars-add-LB-Andy-Studebaker/0de914a3-1ea5-4ba0-abd2-4fb48425d890 |archive-date=April 28, 2018 |access-date=April 27, 2018}}</ref> He was released by the team on September 1, 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jaguars release Shipley, 6 others |url=https://www.bigcatcountry.com/2013/9/1/4683614/jacksonville-jaguars-roster-cuts-kyle-love-jordan-shipley |access-date=April 27, 2018}}</ref>

===Indianapolis Colts (first stint)===
On October 9, 2013, Studebaker signed with the [[Indianapolis Colts]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Alper |first=Josh |date=October 9, 2013 |title=Colts sign Daniel Herron, Andy Studebaker |url=https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2013/10/09/colts-sign-dan-herron-andy-studebaker/ |access-date=March 18, 2021 |website=ProFootballTalk |language=en-US}}</ref> He played in 11 games in 2013.<ref name="stats" /> In 2014, Studebaker played in 13 games, making one start.<ref name="stats" /> He became a free agent at the end of the season.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Josh |date=March 10, 2015 |title=Sounds Like Studebaker Won't Be Returning to Colts |url=https://www.stampedeblue.com/2015/3/10/8184477/it-sounds-like-andy-studebaker-will-not-be-returning-to-the-colts |access-date=March 18, 2021 |website=Stampede Blue |language=en}}</ref>

===Tennessee Titans===
On August 17, 2015, Studebaker signed with the [[Tennessee Titans]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 17, 2015 |title=Titans sign OLB Andy Studebaker, waive WR Clyde Gates |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2015/08/17/titans-sign-olb-andy-studebaker-waive-wr-clyde-davis/31855297/ |access-date=August 17, 2015 |website=usatoday.com |agency=Associated Press}}</ref> He was released by the team on September 4.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 4, 2015 |title=Terry McCormick on Twitter |url=https://twitter.com/terrymc13/status/639814670346526720 |access-date=September 4, 2015 |website=[[Twitter]]}}</ref>

===Indianapolis Colts (second stint)===
On December 15, 2015, Studebaker was signed with the Colts.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Josh |date=December 15, 2015 |title=Colts sign Studebaker, waive Herremans |url=https://www.stampedeblue.com/2015/12/15/10235868/colts-sign-andy-studebaker-waive-todd-herremans-amarlo-herrera |access-date=March 18, 2021 |website=Stampede Blue|publisher=SB Nation |language=en}}</ref> He was released by the team on February 22, 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 22, 2016 |title=Indianapolis Colts make roster moves |url=http://blogs.colts.com/2016/02/22/indianapolis-colts-make-roster-moves-132/ |access-date=February 22, 2016 |website=blogs.colts.com |archive-date=March 6, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306043003/http://blogs.colts.com/2016/02/22/indianapolis-colts-make-roster-moves-132/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>
